products.title: Bucephalandra sp. Green
products.body_html:
This is the unnamed green Bucephalandra — no cultivar label, no premium price, the same plant biology as everything else in the genus. If you want Buce texture across a large piece of hardscape without buying twenty named varieties, start here.

What You'll Receive

Sold as Bunched Plants or Potted Plants:

  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 1-2 plants bundled with a plant weight for easy placement.
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 1-2 plants potted in rockwool and a net pot for secure growth and easy placement.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Green Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp.
  • Also known as — Buce, Bucep
  • Origin — Borneo (genus range)
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Too much light brings algae the plant is too slow to outgrow.
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed. Epiphyte; feeds from the water column.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rhizome creeper; grows submersed or emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Buy this one in quantity. Bucephalandra grows too slowly to cover hardscape on its own — density has to come from how many rhizomes you start with. An unnamed green is the only version of this plant it makes economic sense to buy ten of.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie it to wood or rock and leave it exposed; buried rhizomes rot.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.
  • Leaf color varies plant to plant since this is not a fixed cultivar. Expect a range of greens rather than a uniform batch.
  • Give it flow. Bucephalandra are rheophytes from fast Borneo streams, and moderate current keeps the leaves clean of debris and algae.

products.title: Bucephalandra Achilles Black
products.body_html:
Achilles Black is one of the darkest Bucephalandra varieties in the trade — near-black green leaves that catch blue when light strikes them at an angle. Like every Buce it grows slowly on wood or rock and asks for very little, which is exactly why collectors keep it.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as a Bunched Plants or Potted Plants.
  • Pictures are not the actual plants you will receive, but a sample representation.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Achilles Black Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Achilles Black'
  • Also known as — Buce, Bucep; tribe Schismatoglottideae, family Araceae
  • Origin — Borneo, Indonesia
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed; tie the rhizome to wood or rock
  • Growth habit — Amphibious epiphyte, feeds from roots and water column
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Expect roughly an inch of growth per year. Bucephalandra is one of the slowest plants sold. Most arrive around 2-3 inches and stay close to that for a long time — which is why it holds a scape's composition without trimming.
  • Never bury the rhizome. The horizontal stem must sit in open water, tied to a surface. Buried, it rots, and a plant this slow does not grow back from it in a season.
  • Dark varieties need low light, not none. Strong lighting bleaches the near-black tone toward green and invites algae onto leaves the plant cannot replace quickly. Low to medium light keeps it dark.
  • Look at it from the side. The blue iridescence on dark Buce only shows at an angle. Mounted flat on the substrate and viewed from above, it just reads as a dark green plant.
  • Melt after shipping is normal. Some leaves may drop in the first fortnight while the rhizome settles. Leave it attached and undisturbed — new growth comes from the rhizome, not the old leaves.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Bucephalandra Care Guide.

Notes

  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Bucephalandra Deep Purple Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Deep Purple carries small, slightly wavy oval leaves running dark green through deep violet. It is one of the more reliably purple varieties — the tone holds on emersed and submersed growth alike, where many Buce lose their color on conversion. This is the tissue-culture format.

What You'll Receive

  • One sealed 4-inch Vitro Culture® tissue culture bag
  • Approximately 4 small plantlets grown in sterile nutrient gel
  • 100% free from snails, algae, pesticides and pathogens
  • Rinse the gel away and separate the plantlets before planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Deep Purple Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Deep Purple'
  • Also known as — Buce, Bucep
  • Origin — Borneo (genus range)
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Brighter light intensifies the purple but also brings algae the plant is too slow to outgrow — medium is the practical ceiling.
  • CO₂ — Not required. Deepens color and speeds growth if you already run it.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed. Epiphyte; attaches to wood or rock.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rhizome creeper; grows submersed or emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • The purple survives the switch to submersed growth. Many colored Buce arrive vivid and fade to green in the tank. Deep Purple holds its tone in both forms, which is the practical reason to pick it over a variety that only colors up emersed.
  • Rinse the gel off completely and separate the four plantlets before attaching. Leftover nutrient agar clouds water and feeds algae.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie it to wood or rock and leave it exposed; buried rhizomes rot.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.
  • Moderate flow suits it, mirroring the river conditions the genus comes from and keeping debris off slow-turning leaves.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Bucephalandra Care Guide.

Notes

Remove plants from the tissue culture gel and rinse gently before placing them in your aquarium. Due to the delicate nature of Vitro Culture plants, some melt may occur during transition but will regrow under stable conditions.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Bucephalandra Biblis Blue Sky | Small Vitro Culture Cup
products.body_html:
Blue-violet iridescence on a leaf small enough for a nano. Bucephalandra sp. 'Biblis Blue Sky' shows a metallic blue-purple sheen over deep green, strongest under submerged growth and strong light. The leaves are small and elliptical and the clumps stay compact, which makes it a detail plant rather than a filler.

What You'll Receive

  • One small Vitro Culture® cup, approx. 1.7" × 1.7", containing multiple healthy plantlets in vitamin-enriched gel
  • Tissue culture propagated — free from snails, algae, pathogens and pesticides

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Bucephalandra Blue Sky
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Biblis Blue Sky'
  • Type — Rheophyte / epiphyte
  • Foliage — Deep green with metallic blue and purple iridescence; small elliptical leaves
  • Placement — Foreground, hardscape accents, nano layouts
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Low to medium; higher light deepens the iridescence
  • CO₂ — Not required, though it speeds an already slow plant and holds color better
  • Substrate — Not required. Attach to rock, wood or decor — never bury the rhizome
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • The iridescence is structural, not pigment. It comes from the leaf surface scattering light, which is why it shifts as you move past the tank and why it shows best submerged under strong light. A photograph rarely captures it.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie it to hardscape with the rhizome exposed. Buried, it rots — the single most common way a Buce is lost.
  • Tissue culture makes it safe for shrimp tanks straight out of the cup. Rinse the gel off thoroughly before attaching; residue fouls at the rhizome.
  • Slow growing, so buy roughly the quantity you want. A cup will not fill a scape in a season.
  • Stable water matters more than rich water. Buce sulks and drops leaves after sharp swings in temperature or chemistry.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.

products.title: Hygrophila Pinnatifida
products.body_html:
Deeply lobed, fern-like leaves that run bronze to reddish-brown under stronger light — unlike any other stem plant in the hobby. It's also a rheophyte, so it can be planted in substrate or tied to wood and stone like an Anubias.

What You’ll Receive

Choose from a variety of planting formats to suit your layout:

  • Small Bare-Root Plants: Includes 1 small rooted plant, perfect for attaching to driftwood, stones, or décor.
  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 2–3 fresh-cut stems without roots for flexible planting arrangements.
  • Fresh-Cut Bunched: 2–3 fresh-cut stems bundled with foam and a plant weight for quick placement.
  • Fresh-Cut Potted: 2–3 fresh-cut stems securely potted in rockwool and a net pot for stability and continued growth.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pinnatifida, Hygrophila Pinnatifida
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila pinnatifida
  • Origin — India
  • Placement — Midground, planted or on hardscape
  • Shipped size — 1 small rooted plant, or 2-3 fresh-cut stems roughly 2-4 in
  • Mature height — 4–10 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Low to medium. It grows in low light; the bronze and red need stronger light
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required if attached to hardscape; nutrient substrate if planted
  • Growth habit — Rheophyte. Plants in substrate or attaches to wood and stone
  • Propagation — Cuttings and side shoots

Grower’s Notes

  • It behaves like two different plants. Tied to wood or stone it creeps sideways and throws vertical shoots like an epiphyte. Planted in substrate it grows taller and greener. Decide which you want before you place it.
  • Pinholes in older leaves mean potassium. This plant is unusually hungry for it and shows the deficiency before anything else in the tank does — treat it as an early warning for your dosing.
  • Bronze and red develop under strong light with iron available. In low light it stays green and healthy — the color is a lighting response, not a health sign.
  • It drops lower leaves as it lengthens. Cut the tops and replant them rather than waiting for the bare stems to fill back in.
  • Also available as sterile Pinnatifida Vitro Culture, and as the compact 'UK' form.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Hygrophila Pinnatifida Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference; leaf color, size and form vary considerably with lighting and nutrients. Grown emersed and will transition to submersed growth after planting.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Java Fern Thor's Hammer
products.body_html:
Leaf tips that flare out into a blunt hammer shape. Leptochilus pteropus 'Thor's Hammer' is one of the more sculptural Java Fern forms — the silhouette does the work, so it reads as a feature plant even in a tank with no CO₂ and no bright light.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose bare-root plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Bare-root Plants: Approximately 3+ leaf portion, loose rhizome
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 3+ leaf portion bundled with foam and plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 3+ leaf portion, potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Thor's Hammer Java Fern
  • Scientific name — Leptochilus pteropus 'Thor's Hammer' (syn. Microsorum pteropus)
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Midground, attached to driftwood, stone or décor
  • Mature height — 6-10 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5, soft to moderately hard
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte — tie the rhizome to hardscape and never bury it.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; grows emersed as well as submersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division, plus plantlets from mature leaves

Grower's Notes

  • Expect a change of leaf. We grow this emersed, so some of the fronds it arrives with will yellow and drop as the plant converts to submerged growth. The rhizome is what matters — leave it alone and new, correctly-formed leaves follow.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots may go into substrate; the thick horizontal stem must stay in open water or it rots. This is the single most common way a Java Fern is killed.
  • Black spots on old leaves are baby plants, not disease. Java Fern reproduces by growing plantlets along the leaf margins. Leave a spotted leaf in place until each plantlet has roots and two or three leaves, then detach and attach it elsewhere.
  • Keep the light low. It grows slowly enough that strong lighting mostly feeds algae on the leaves. Shade gives cleaner, darker fronds and sharper leaf tips.
  • It feeds from the water, not the substrate. Root tabs do nothing here. A basic liquid fertilizer is all it needs, and even that is optional in a stocked tank.

products.title: Ceratopteris Siliquosa
products.body_html:
Want a fast plant that propagates itself? Water Sprite grows fine, lacy fern foliage that fills a background in weeks — planted or floating, your choice — and produces new plants along its own leaf margins with no effort from you.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as Fresh-cut Plants, Bunched Plants or Potted Plants:

  • Fresh-cut Plants: Approximately 6 loose fresh-cut plants without root.
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 6 fresh-cut plants without root bundled with a plant weight for easy placement.
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 6 fresh-cut plants without root potted in rockwool and a net pot for secure growth and easy placement.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Water Sprite, Narrow Leaf Water Sprite
  • Scientific name — Ceratopteris thalictroides 'Siliquosa'
  • Placement — Midground to background, or floating
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Feeds mainly from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Plantlets on leaf margins

Grower’s Notes

  • It clones itself along its leaves. Small plantlets form on the leaf edges and on older leaves as they age. Once one has a few fronds and roots, detach it and plant or float it — this is how a single portion becomes a tankful without you doing anything.
  • Planted or floating are both correct. Floating it grows faster and shades the tank below; planted it grows more upright. Floating is the usual choice in fry and shrimp tanks.
  • It strips nitrate quickly, which makes it genuinely useful in a new or heavily stocked tank rather than just decorative.
  • Roots are fragile when planted. Bury only enough to hold it and let it anchor itself, or it tears loose.

Water Sprite is not Water Wisteria. This is a true fern, growing as a rosette and reproducing from leaf plantlets. Water Wisteria is Hygrophila difformis — a flowering stem plant with paired leaves up an upright stem. Both have finely divided foliage, which is where the confusion starts.

products.title: Cryptocoryne Spiralis
products.body_html:
Cryptocoryne spiralis looks nothing like the rest of the genus. Instead of broad wendtii-style leaves it sends up long, narrow ribbons that twist as they rise, giving the sway of Vallisneria with the low-light tolerance of a crypt. It is one of the few background plants that asks for no CO₂ and no strong lighting.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as a Bare-root Plants, or Potted Plants
  • Young plants grow in a controlled laboratory environment

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Spiralis Crypt
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne spiralis
  • Also known as — Spiral water trumpet, Indian crypt
  • Origin — India and Sri Lanka
  • Placement — Background
  • Mature height — 8-14 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; plant the crown at substrate level
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette, root feeder
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower's Notes

  • The melt is not the plant dying. Crypts shed their existing leaves after any move or parameter change and regrow from the crown. Leave the roots in place, resist replanting, and new submersed leaves appear in three to six weeks.
  • It feeds through its roots. Water column dosing does little here. Root tabs or an enriched substrate under the crown are what produce full-length ribbon leaves rather than short, pale ones.
  • Use it where Vallisneria would be too aggressive. Spiralis gives similar vertical movement in the background but spreads by slow runners instead of taking over a tank in a season.
  • Leave it alone once established. Frequent uprooting resets the melt cycle. Choose the spot before planting and let the runners fill in around it.
  • Stable water beats ideal water. Spiralis tolerates a wide pH and hardness range but reacts to sudden swings. Consistent weekly water changes matter more than hitting an exact number.

products.title: Microsorum Pteropus Trident
products.body_html:
Want Java Fern with a finer silhouette? Trident splits each leaf into narrow forked fingers instead of a single broad blade — more movement, more detail, and it reads far lighter on hardscape than standard Java Fern. Same near-indestructible plant underneath.

What You’ll Receive

Fresh, healthy Leptochilus pteropus 'Trident' cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in convenient planting formats:

Bare-root Plants: Approximately 3+ leaves per portion with loose rhizome and attached roots
Bunched Plants: Approximately 3+ leaves per portion bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement
Potted Plants: Approximately 3+ leaves per portion potted in a net pot with rockwool for stability and easy planting

Each portion may consist of individual leaves with separated rhizome sections, which is completely natural for this species. All pieces are viable and will continue to grow once placed in your aquarium.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Trident Java Fern
  • Scientific name — Leptochilus pteropus 'Trident' (formerly Microsorum pteropus)
  • Placement — Midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 6–10 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light means algae on slow-turning leaves
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape and feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division, plus plantlets on mature leaves

Grower’s Notes

  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie it to wood or rock with cotton thread or fishing line, rhizome fully exposed — buried in substrate it rots, and this is how most Java Ferns are lost.
  • It clones itself. Small plantlets form along the edges and tips of mature leaves. Once one has a few leaves and visible roots, snap it off and attach it elsewhere — this is how a single portion becomes a wall of fern over a year.
  • Black spots on older leaves are usually plantlet sites or normal aging, not disease. If whole leaves brown from the base, look at light and flow instead.
  • Trident grows faster and stays narrower than standard Java Fern, which makes it easier to use in smaller tanks without it swamping the hardscape.

products.title: Salvinia Minima
products.body_html:
Need nitrate gone and algae starved out fast? Salvinia Minima does it quicker than almost anything. Small quilted leaves with water-repellent hairs spread across the surface, soaking up nutrients and shading the tank below — and it grows fast enough that thinning it becomes a weekly job.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a small portion
  • Approx. 2" x 2" in size

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Salvinia Minima, Water Spangles
  • Scientific name — Salvinia minima
  • Plant type — Floating fern
  • Placement — Floating on the surface
  • Mature height — 0.5–1 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner. Close to unkillable
  • Light — Medium to high, though it manages on less
  • CO₂ — Not required! It takes carbon straight from the air
  • Water — 65–85°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Feeding — Water column
  • Propagation — Runners; it multiplies on its own

Grower’s Notes

  • Thin it every week. This is the fastest-spreading plant we sell, and left alone it forms a solid mat that shades out everything beneath it.
  • The leaf hairs repel water, so it tolerates surface movement far better than Red Root Floater or Frogbit — a good choice if your filter breaks the surface.
  • Yellowing usually means iron or micronutrients. Floating plants feed entirely from the water column and show a deficiency before rooted plants do.
  • Bigger sister plant: if you want the same look at three times the leaf size, see Salvinia Natans.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference; portion size and leaf density vary with growing conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Rotala Rotundifolia Green
products.body_html:
Want a stem plant that stays green? Most Rotala redden under strong light — Rotala rotundifolia 'Green' does not. It holds a bright, consistent green whatever you throw at it, which makes it the reliable contrast against red plants rather than another competitor for the same color.

What You’ll Receive

Fresh, healthy Rotala Rotundifolia Green cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in convenient planting formats:

Fresh Cut Plants: Approximately 6+ loose, fresh-cut stems without roots.
Fresh Cut Bunched: Approximately 6+ stems bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.
Fresh Cut Potted: About 6+ stems potted securely in a net pot with rockwool for stability and easy planting.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Rotala Green, Rotala Indica Green
  • Scientific name — Rotala rotundifolia 'Green'
  • Origin — Southeast Asia (species range)
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Approx. 6+ fresh-cut stems, roughly 4-8 in
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Not required. Denser and faster with it, but not needed
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Stem cuttings

Grower’s Notes

  • The leaves change shape completely. Grown above water the leaves are round and coin-like; submerged they become narrow and elongated. Nursery stock arrives in the emersed form, so the plant that grows in will not look like the one you planted. This is normal and catches people out.
  • It responds better to trimming than almost any stem plant. Cut it and each stem branches into two, which is how a few stems become a dense hedge.
  • Replant the trimmed tops rather than keeping bare lower stems — tops root within days.
  • Plant stems a little apart. Packed tight the inner stems shade out and drop their lower leaves.
  • Unlike the standard rotundifolia, no amount of light will turn this one pink. If you want color from this genus, that is the plant to buy instead — 'Green' is here to be green.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference only. Leaf shape, height, and density may vary depending on lighting, nutrients, CO₂ levels, and aquarium conditions. Minor melting after planting is normal as the plant transitions to submerged growth.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Mini Christmas Moss
products.body_html:
Want the Christmas Moss shape at nano scale? Mini Christmas Moss branches into the same triangular fir-tree fronds as the standard form, at roughly half the size — which means the pattern stays visible on small hardscape instead of reading as a green blur.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as small, loose portion
  • Approx. 2 inches in size

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Mini Christmas Moss, also known as Mini Xmas Moss
  • Scientific name — Vesicularia montagnei 'Mini'
  • Also known as — Taxiphyllum sp. 'Mini Christmas', Vesicularia sp. 'Mini Christmas'
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. High light grows algae, not moss
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5. Cooler water gives tighter branching
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Fragmentation

Grower’s Notes

  • Cooler water keeps the shape. Like standard Christmas Moss, the tight triangular branching is a cool-water trait. In a warm tank it grows looser and longer and starts to look like ordinary Java Moss — the small size makes that loss more obvious, not less.
  • Attach a thin layer, not a thick pad. A dense clump rots underneath where no light or flow reaches, and the whole piece lets go.
  • Trim regularly. Each cut forces branching, which is what keeps the fir-tree structure crisp rather than stringy.
  • Never bury it in substrate, and never let algae establish — there is no safe way to remove algae from moss.

products.title: Alternanthera Reineckii 'Super Magenta'
products.body_html:
Want magenta rather than plain red? Alternanthera reineckii 'Super Magenta' runs deeper into pink and purple than standard AR, and holds it further down the stem. It is the strongest color contrast you can put next to a green background without resorting to a difficult plant.

What You’ll Receive

Enhance your aquarium with our fresh, high-quality plants, available in three convenient formats:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Includes approximately 5+ loose, fresh-cut stems without roots – perfect for custom placement
  • Fresh-Cut Bunched: About 5+ fresh-cut stems bundled with foam and plant weight – ideal for easy setup
  • Fresh-Cut Potted: Approximately 5+ fresh-cut stems potted in rockwool and net pot – ready to anchor and grow

Plant Profile

products.title: Ludwigia Super Red Mini
products.body_html:
The "Mini" in the name is about the leaf, not the plant. Ludwigia palustris 'Super Red' in its mini form carries the same deep crimson as standard Super Red on leaves a fraction of the size — but left untrimmed, the stem grows just as tall as any other Ludwigia. It's also one of the easier red stem plants to color: it turns red reliably even under medium light, and stays a forgiving, beginner-friendly plant overall.

  • Needs a nutrient-rich substrate to look its best. No enriched substrate on hand is fine too — a liquid nutrient or fertilizer covers the gap.

products.title: Taiwan Moss
products.body_html:
The moss that drapes tidily. Taxiphyllum alternans — Taiwan Moss — grows in overlapping, downward-angled fronds rather than the shapeless tangle Java Moss makes, so a planted piece of wood keeps a defined silhouette as it fills in. One of the easiest mosses to make look deliberate.

  • Common name — Taiwan Moss
  • Scientific name — Taxiphyllum alternans
  • Placement — Midground, attached to driftwood, stone or décor

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner

products.title: Willow Moss
products.body_html:
The moss for cold tanks. Fontinalis antipyretica — Willow Moss — comes from cool, clear streams across the Northern Hemisphere and prefers water between 60 and 75°F. In an unheated or lightly heated tank, where tropical mosses sulk, this one thrives — growing long, flowing, willow-like fronds off rock and driftwood.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as a loose portion approximately 2" x 2" — ready to tie or attach to any surface using thread or mesh. Each portion may vary slightly in shape and density due to natural variation.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Willow Moss
  • Scientific name — Fontinalis antipyretica
  • Origin — Cool streams and lakes, Northern Hemisphere
  • Placement — Midground, attached to rock, driftwood or mesh
  • Mature height — 4–10 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Thrives in shade
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 60–75°F · pH 6.0–7.5. Note the ceiling — this is a cold-water moss
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — True aquatic. Does not grow emersed
  • Propagation — Fragmentation — divide and re-attach

Grower’s Notes

  • The temperature range is the reason to buy it. Most aquarium mosses want tropical warmth. Willow Moss wants 60–75°F — which makes it one of the very few mosses that works in a goldfish tank, an unheated room-temperature setup, or a coldwater biotope.
  • Above 78–80°F it thins and browns. In a tropical community tank, use Java Moss or Christmas Moss instead.
  • Tie it on thinly with cotton thread. Thick mats trap detritus and rot from underneath; a thin layer grows across the surface.
  • Flowing fronds give shrimp and fry excellent cover and a large surface for biofilm.
  • Arriving compressed and dark is normal. Rinse gently, place it in clean water, and color returns within days.

products.title: Weeping Moss
products.body_html:
Want moss that hangs rather than sprawls? Weeping Moss grows downward. Its fronds cascade from wherever you attach them, which makes it the moss of choice for branch tips and overhangs where you want a drooping, willow-like effect nothing else gives you.

  • Perfect to attached to driftwood, rock, or stone

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Weeping Moss
  • Scientific name — Vesicularia ferriei
  • Plant type — Rheophyte, epiphytic moss
  • Placement — Midground, on wood or stone

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner

  • CO₂ — Not required! Denser and faster with it, perfectly happy without
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Feeding — Water column; the rhizoids anchor only, they don't feed

  • Trim the trailing tips to keep it dense. Left alone the strands lengthen and thin out, losing the full weeping look.
  • Gentle flow keeps it clean. The fine fronds trap detritus in still water and brown from the inside.

products.title: Snowflake Moss
products.body_html:
Snowflake Moss grows in flat, triangular fronds that fan out like the shape it is named for — nothing else in the moss range looks like it. It is also one of the slowest, which is the trade-off: a distinctive plant that takes its time and needs keeping clean.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as a small loose portion
  • Rare & uncommon moss
  • Approx. 2" x 2" in size
  • Perfect to attached to driftwood, rock, or stone

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Snowflake Moss
  • Scientific name — Thuidium sp. 'Snowflake'
  • Also known as — Snowflake Thuidium
  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Midground; attaches to driftwood, stone or decor
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed; feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious epiphyte
  • Propagation — Fragmentation

Grower's Notes

  • Slow growth means algae is the real enemy. A moss this slow cannot outgrow algae settling on its fronds. Amano or cherry shrimp, otocinclus or nerite snails keep it clean far more effectively than manual cleaning — and a grazing crew is close to essential for this one.
  • It is a Thuidium, not a Vesicularia. Snowflake Moss is sometimes listed under the wrong genus. That matters when you search for care advice — Vesicularia mosses like Christmas Moss are faster and more forgiving than this one.
  • Cooler water suits it. It holds its shape better at the lower end of the range. Run warm and it thins out and traps more debris.
  • Attach it thin, not thick. Spread a single layer over wood or mesh. A thick pad shades its own base, which browns and lets go — and on a moss this slow that loss takes months to recover.
  • Keep flow across it. Moss in dead water collects detritus, and detritus is what algae grows on. Moderate current does most of the maintenance for you.

products.title: Pearl Moss
products.body_html:
Want a moss that doesn't look like moss? Pearl Moss grows rounded, translucent leaves arranged along creeping stems — large enough to see individually, catching light like small pearls. It reads far more like a miniature land plant than the fine tangle of Java or Christmas moss.

What You’ll Receive

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pearl Moss
  • Scientific name — Plagiomnium cf. affine
  • Placement — Midground, attached to wood or stone
  • Mature height — 2–4 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner

products.title: Phoenix Moss (Fissidens Fontanus)
products.body_html:
Looking for a moss that stays neat instead of going stringy? Phoenix Moss is it. Deep dark green fronds grow in tight, feathery fans that hug whatever you attach them to — slow, compact, and far tidier than Java Moss, which is exactly why aquascapers pay more for it.

What You’ll Receive

  • Dark Green Moss
  • Sold as a small portion, loose moss
  • Approx. 2" x 2" / 5cm x 5cm in size
  • Perfect to attach to driftwood, rock, or stone

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Phoenix Moss, US Fissidens
  • Scientific name — Fissidens fontanus
  • Color — Dark green
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner to keep, though slow to establish
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light invites algae it cannot outgrow
  • CO₂ — Not required! But CO₂ with cooler water brings out a noticeably greener, denser growth
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5; cooler is better for color
  • Feeding — Water column
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic. This moss cannot be grown emersed
  • Propagation — Fragmentation; every piece grows into a new fan

Grower’s Notes

  • It must stay submerged. Unlike most mosses we sell, Fissidens fontanus has no emersed form — it is not suited to wabi-kusa, paludariums or dry start, and will not survive out of water.
  • CO₂ and cooler water are what make it green. Without them it still grows perfectly well, just darker and slower — the vivid green in aquascaping photos comes from injected tanks running on the cool side.
  • Tie it on in a thin, even layer. Phoenix Moss grows slowly, so a thick pad shades and rots underneath long before the top fills in.
  • Flow matters more than light. The fine fronds trap detritus in still water — gentle current keeps them clean.
  • Be patient. It attaches and spreads far slower than Java Moss, taking a couple of months to knit onto hardscape. That slowness is why it holds its shape.

products.title: Mini Pellia / Mini Coral Moss
products.body_html:
Want texture nothing else in the hobby can give you? Mini Pellia grows in finely branched, deep green fronds that look like miniature coral — dense compact cushions rather than the loose strands of a true moss. It is a liverwort, and it is the detail plant serious aquascapers reach for.

What You’ll Receive

  • Loose Portion: Approximately 2" × 2"
  • Ready to Attach: Suitable for rocks, driftwood, mesh, or other aquarium décor

Portion size and density may vary slightly because this is a natural live plant.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Mini Pellia, Mini Coral Moss, Mini Liverwort
  • Scientific name — Riccardia chamedryfolia
  • Plant type — Liverwort, not a true moss
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on wood, stone or mesh
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate. Not hard, but slow and unforgiving of neglect
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required, but it rewards CO₂ more than most mosses do
  • Water — Cooler is better; it thrives below about 75°F and struggles in warm tanks
  • Feeding — Water column
  • Propagation — Fragmentation; reattach healthy clippings

Grower’s Notes

  • Temperature is the deciding factor. Riccardia is a cool-water plant — in a tank running above 78°F it thins, browns and slowly gives up no matter how good the light and CO₂ are.
  • Flow matters more than light. The dense fronds trap detritus in still water and rot from the inside, so give it gentle, steady circulation.
  • Tie it on thin and flat. A thick clump smothers itself long before the surface fills in, and this plant is far too slow to recover from that.
  • It attaches slowly. Expect a couple of months before it grips hardscape properly — keep the thread or mesh on until it does.
  • Not to be confused with plain Pellia (Monosolenium tenerum), which is thicker, faster, more brittle and far more heat tolerant.

products.title: Flame Moss
products.body_html:

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Flame Moss
  • Scientific name — Taxiphyllum sp. 'Flame'
  • Also known as — Vesicularia sp. 'Flame'
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 2–4 in of upright growth
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light brings algae it grows too slowly to shed
  • CO₂ — Not required! Tighter and faster with it, perfectly happy without
  • Water — 70–82°F · pH 5.0–8.0, one of the widest ranges of any plant
  • Feeding — Water column
  • Propagation — Fragmentation; divide and reattach small sections

Grower’s Notes

  • Tie it in a thin, flat layer and let it rise on its own. The vertical growth is what you are paying for, and a thick clump smothers that shape before it forms.
  • Cooler water gives tighter flames. In warm tanks the fronds loosen and lengthen, losing the twisting column look.
  • Trim the tops rather than the sides. Cutting the tips forces new upright shoots and keeps the flame effect dense.
  • Be patient. It is slow even by moss standards and takes a couple of months to knit onto hardscape — that slowness is why it holds its shape so well.

Fresh Cut Bunched: Approximately 6+ stems bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.
Fresh Cut Potted: About 6+ stems potted securely in a net pot with rockwool for stability and easy planting.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Mayaca, Bog Moss, Stream Bogmoss
  • Scientific name — Mayaca fluviatilis
  • Origin — South and Central America

  • Mature height — 6–14 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Stronger light tightens the internodes and thickens growth
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.0
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Stem cuttings

Grower’s Notes

  • Soft water is the requirement people miss. Mayaca does noticeably better in soft, slightly acidic water and struggles in hard alkaline tap. If it thins and pales despite good light and dosing, water chemistry is usually the reason.
  • Handle it by the base. The fine foliage strips off where you grip the stem, and those bare nodes do not refoliate.
  • Plant stems a little apart and let them fill in. Packed tight, the inner stems shade out and shed from the bottom.
  • Trim and replant the tops. Bare lower sections are not worth keeping on a plant grown for its texture.
  • The fine leaves trap detritus and suit hair algae. Keep flow moving through the stand and remove affected stems promptly.

products.title: Java Moss Coconut Cave
products.body_html:
A half coconut shell already grown over with Java Moss — shelter and planting in one piece. Shrimp graze the moss, fry hide inside the shell, and plecos and small catfish use it as a cave. Drop it in and it works immediately.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Java Moss
  • Scientific name — Taxiphyllum barbieri
  • Also known as — long sold under the misapplied name Vesicularia dubyana
  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Foreground to midground; sits on the substrate
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed; feeds from the water column

Grower's Notes

  • It is a breeding tank in one object. Fry that make it into the shell are out of reach of adults, and the moss outside holds the microfauna they feed on. That combination is why coconut caves outperform plain ceramic ones for shrimp and small fish.
  • Cooler water keeps the moss tidy. Java Moss is happiest at the lower end of its range. Above about 80°F the shoots stretch, thin out and trap more debris.
  • Trim the surface to thicken it. Cutting the moss back with scissors forces branching lower down. Left alone it grows long and stringy and the shell shows through.
  • Keep some flow across it. Moss in still water collects detritus, and detritus is what algae grows on. Moderate current keeps it clean without needing to be handled.

products.title: Vallisneria Americana
products.body_html:
Want Vallisneria that won't take over the tank? Corkscrew Val stays 8 to 12 inches instead of running to the surface, and twists its blades along their whole length into tight spirals. Of our three twisted Vals, this is the one with the widest blade — the spirals read boldly rather than as fine threads.

What You’ll Receive

  • Bare-root Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual loose, bare-root plants
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual bare-root plants bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual bare-root plants potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Corkscrew Val, also known as Twisted Val
  • Scientific name — Vallisneria americana 'Asiatica'
  • Origin — Asia (this cultivar); the species is North American
  • Placement — Midground, or foreground in a large tank
  • Shipped size — Approx. 2-3 bare-root plants, roughly 4-8 in
  • Mature height — 8–12 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Brighter light tightens the spiral
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–8.0. Tolerates hard, alkaline water well
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Wide blades, mid height. Jungle Val and spiralis keep growing until they hit the surface and trail along it. 'Asiatica' tops out around a foot, which is why it works where taller Vallisneria would swamp the layout.
  • Plant the crown at the substrate line, never below it. A buried crown rots — the usual reason a new Val fails in the first fortnight.
  • Feed at the roots. In inert gravel it survives but barely spreads; root tabs are what turn three plants into a colony.
  • Don't trim the tops to control height. Cut Val leaves brown at the cut and stay that way. Remove whole leaves at the base instead.
  • Runners travel fast. Pull unwanted plantlets by hand rather than cutting, and expect to thin it every month or two once established.

products.title: Anubias Petite White Panda | Small Vitro Culture Cup
products.body_html:
Heart-shaped leaves split between white and green. Anubias 'Petite White Panda' is among the rarest Anubias in the hobby and among the hardest to keep — the two facts are related. This is the small tissue culture cup, grown in our own lab in the USA.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as Tissue Culture Plants in 1 oz cup
  • APF premium product, grown in our lab in USA
  • One of the rarest Anubias species on the market

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Petite White Panda Anubias
  • Scientific name — Anubias barteri var. nana 'Petite White Panda'
  • Origin — Cultivated variegated form; the genus is native to West and Central Africa
  • Placement — Midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 1-3 inches
  • Growth rate — Very slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light scorches the white tissue and feeds algae.
  • CO₂ — Not required. Stability matters far more than any additive.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte — attach the rhizome to hardscape and never bury it.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • This is not an easy plant, and the reason is chlorophyll. White areas of the leaf cannot photosynthesize, so a heavily marked Panda runs on a fraction of the energy a green Anubias makes. Expect very slow growth, poor recovery from damage, and no ability to outgrow algae. It rewards a stable, well-run tank rather than a bright one.
  • It can revert. Under weak light or thin feeding the plant may start pushing plain green leaves. Remove them promptly — green growth photosynthesizes better and will out-compete the marked tissue if left.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots can go into substrate; the rhizome cannot. Buried, it rots, and this plant will not recover from that.
  • Rinse the gel off with aquarium or dechlorinated water, not tap, before attaching.
  • Place one as a feature rather than several as a group. At this price and this size, a single well-lit-but-shaded specimen against dark hardscape does more than a scattered handful.

products.title: Vallisneria Gigantea
products.body_html:
Want a green curtain rather than a background plant? Vallisneria gigantea reaches two to four feet, sending broad ribbon leaves to the surface and trailing them along it. In a big open-top tank the effect is genuinely dramatic — in a standard tank it simply takes over.

Size matters here: this needs 40 gallons and real depth. For a smaller tank choose Vallisneria Nana or Vallisneria Torta instead.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as loose fresh-cut plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Bare-root Plants: Approximately 1–2 individual loose, bare-root plants
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 1–2 individual bare-root plants bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 1–2 individual bare-root plants potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Giant Val, also known as Giant Vallisneria
  • Scientific name — Vallisneria gigantea
  • Origin — Southeast Asia and Australia
  • Placement — Background
  • Shipped size — Approx. 1-2 bare-root plants, roughly 8-14 in
  • Mature height — 24–48 in
  • Suits — 40 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–8.0. Tolerates hard, alkaline water well
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Plant the crown at the substrate line, never below it. A buried crown rots — the usual reason a new Val fails in the first fortnight.
  • Feed at the roots. In inert gravel it survives but barely spreads; root tabs are what turn two plants into a curtain.
  • Don't trim the tops to control height. Cut Val leaves brown at the cut and stay that way — remove whole leaves at the base instead.

products.title: Amazon Frogbit
products.body_html:
Fighting algae or want cover for fry and shrimp? Amazon Frogbit does both at once. Round, spongy leaves sit on the surface while long hair-like roots trail down into the water column — stripping the nitrate algae wants, shading the tank below, and giving shrimplets somewhere to hide.

What You’ll Receive

Fresh, healthy Amazon Frogbit cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®. Choose the pack size that suits your tank:

  • 3 Plants — Starter Pack. For nano tanks under 10 gallons, or anyone who would rather buy a small culture and let it multiply. Frogbit grows fast, so a few plants become a mat within weeks.
  • 6 Plants — Standard Pack. The usual choice for a 10 to 20 gallon tank. Enough to look established from the start without covering the whole surface on day one.
  • 12 Plants — Value / Breeder Pack. For tanks of 40 gallons and up, or breeders who need cover for fry immediately rather than waiting for the plants to spread.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Amazon Frogbit
  • Scientific name — Limnobium laevigatum
  • Also known as — South American Spongeplant, Smooth Frogbit
  • Origin — Central and South America
  • Placement — Floating on the surface
  • Shipped size — 3, 6 or 12 individual plants depending on pack
  • Mature height — Floats; roots trail several inches down
  • Suits — 5 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner. One of the easiest plants you can buy
  • Light — Low to medium is plenty; it sits closest to the light already
  • CO₂ — Not required. It takes carbon straight from the air
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — None. It floats and feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic floater
  • Propagation — Runners; daughter plants appear on their own

Grower’s Notes

  • Keep the leaf tops dry. Water sitting on the leaves makes them yellow and rot, so aim filter outflow below the surface and skip the airstone underneath it. This is the single most common way frogbit fails.
  • Leave an air gap under the lid. Condensation dripping back down does exactly the same damage as spray.
  • Buy for where you want to end up, not where you start. Three plants will reach the coverage of twelve in a month or so under decent light. Pay for the larger pack only if you need the shade or the fry cover now.
  • Thin it every week or two. It doubles fast, and a solid mat of frogbit will shade out every plant beneath it — half to two-thirds surface cover is a sensible target.
  • Yellowing leaves usually mean iron or micronutrients, not light. Floating plants feed entirely from the water column and are the first to show a deficiency.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference; leaf size and root length vary with lighting and nutrient availability. Not suitable for tanks with strong surface agitation or high flow.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: American Frogbit
products.body_html:
Miniature lily pads that need no planting. Limnobium spongia — American Frogbit — floats round, glossy leaves on the surface with a curtain of fine roots trailing beneath. Native to North America, undemanding, and one of the few floaters that looks deliberate rather than weedy.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as a small portion – approx. 1–2 individual plants

Plant Profile

  • Common name — American Frogbit
  • Scientific name — Limnobium spongia
  • Origin — North America
  • Placement — Free-floating on the surface
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required. It takes CO₂ from the air
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed on wet margins

  • Keep the leaves dry on top. Frogbit hates water landing on its leaves — condensation from a tight lid or spray from a filter return makes the tops rot. An open top or a small gap under the lid solves it, and it's the single most common reason Frogbit fails.

  • Thin it regularly — daughter plants form fast and a sealed surface starves plants below of light.
  • Compare with Amazon Frogbit: similar habit, larger leaves, tropical rather than North American.

Notes

products.body_html:

Monosolenium tenerum — Pellia — is a liverwort that grows broad ribbon-like fronds rather than fine filaments, forming dense dark green cushions with real substance. Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pellia
  • Scientific name — Monosolenium tenerum
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on wood, stone or mesh

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to wood, stone or mesh

  • Trim it often. Regular trims keep moss dense and stop the lower layers from rotting.
  • This one is fully aquatic and cannot be grown out of water, so it is not suited to a terrarium or the dry start method.

products.title: Water Mimosa
products.body_html:
Want a plant that reacts when you touch it? Water Mimosa folds its delicate fern-like leaflets inward within seconds of being disturbed, then opens again once left alone. It floats on spongy buoyant stems, forming a soft green canopy — and it is the only plant we sell that moves on its own.

What You’ll Receive

Healthy Water Mimosa plants carefully prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®.

Variants available:

2 Plants – Unrooted
Fresh-cut floating plants without roots.

2 Plants – Rooted
Fresh-cut floating plants with visible developing roots.

10 Plants – Unrooted
Bulk portion of fresh-cut floating plants without roots.

10 Plants – Rooted
Bulk portion of fresh-cut floating plants with visible developing roots.

All plants are carefully selected and shipped fresh to ensure healthy arrival.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Water Mimosa, also known as Sensitive Water Mimosa
  • Scientific name — Neptunia oleracea
  • Placement — Floating
  • Mature height — 6–8 in above the surface
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 70–85°F · pH 6.5–7.5. Warmth matters more than most floaters
  • Substrate — Not required. Feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also roots in pond margins
  • Propagation — Plantlets along trailing stems

Grower’s Notes

  • The leaf movement is real and repeatable. Touch, vibration or a sudden change in light causes the leaflets to fold within a second or two, reopening over the next few minutes. It is the same mechanism as the terrestrial sensitive plant.
  • Keep the foliage dry. Like other floaters, the leaves sit above the waterline and rot if constantly splashed — aim filter outflow below the surface.
  • It wants warmth. Growth slows markedly at the cool end of its range, so this is a poor choice for an unheated tank.
  • Propagate by separating plantlets that form along the trailing stems and floating them on. It spreads quickly enough to need thinning.
  • Expect folded leaves on arrival. Transit stress makes it close up; it reopens within a day of being floated in stable conditions.

  • Aquatic plants may experience minor cosmetic changes during shipping due to temperature, handling, and transit time. Leaves may temporarily fold or show slight stress but typically recover quickly once placed in suitable aquarium or pond conditions.

products.title: Java Fern Petite Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Java Fern at 2 to 4 inches. Leptochilus pteropus 'Petite' is the dwarf form — narrow, arching leaves on a plant small enough for a nano tank or a bonsai branch, where the standard fern would swamp the layout. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You'll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing 2–3 small clumps of Java Fern 'Petite', ready for immediate use in your aquascape.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Petite Java Fern
  • Scientific name — Leptochilus pteropus 'Petite' (syn. Microsorum pteropus)
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, attached to driftwood, stone or décor
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte — attach the rhizome to hardscape and never bury it.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; grows emersed as well as submersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division, plus plantlets from mature leaves

Grower's Notes

  • Petite stays petite. Unlike a "small size" grade of a large plant, this is a genuinely dwarf cultivar — it will not grow into a standard Java Fern. That is what makes it the right choice for a nano tank rather than a temporary fix.
  • Rinse every trace of gel off before planting. Tissue culture plants arrive in sterile nutrient gel. Any left on the roots feeds a bacterial bloom — rinse under room-temperature water until the roots feel clean, then divide the clumps.
  • Attach the clumps close together. Two or three small clumps look sparse on their own. Grouped on one piece of wood they read as a single established plant within a few months.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots may go into substrate; the green horizontal stem must stay in open water or it rots — the single most common way a Java Fern is killed.
  • Sterile media is the point. No snails, no algae spores, no pesticide residue — which is why this format suits shrimp tanks where a conventionally farmed plant is a real risk.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Java Fern Care Guide.

Notes

Photos are for reference only. Leaf size and shape may vary based on tank conditions. Avoid burying the rhizome—attach only to hard surfaces to prevent rot. Tissue-culture plants may appear smaller than mature aquarium plants and fill out once established.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Bucephalandra Species on Coco Pad [Grower's Choice]
products.body_html:
Attaching Bucephalandra is the slow part — tying rhizomes to wood, waiting months for them to grip. This is that work already done. A mixed Buce planting grown into a natural coconut-shell pad, ready to drop straight into a tank and move around until it looks right.

What You'll Receive

Grower's Choice Bucephalandra species meaning we will randomly pick the species for you. We do not take requests for specific species or colors. Each order is randomly picked with one mystery species. It may be a bit bigger or smaller in size depending on the variety. We do not label or identify the species.

You will get 1 pad with many rhizomes of Bucephalandra. This is a HUGE-SAVING compared to buying an individual rhizome. We do not take requests for specific species or colors. Each piece is randomly picked, with random varieties and a unique shape that approx. 1x2 inches in size. It may be a bit bigger or smaller in size depending on the variety.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Buce, Bucep
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. (Grower's Choice)
  • Also known as — Tribe Schismatoglottideae, family Araceae
  • Origin — Borneo, Indonesia
  • Placement — Foreground to midground; sits on the substrate or on hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed; the pad sits on top and the rhizomes stay in open water
  • Growth habit — Amphibious epiphyte, feeds from roots and water column
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Do not bury the pad. Set it on the substrate or wedge it between rocks. Pushing it under gravel buries the rhizomes underneath, and buried Buce rhizomes rot.
  • It is meant to be moved. The whole point of a pad is that you can lift it, reposition it, or take it out for a water change without disturbing anything else. Use that — try it in a few spots before deciding.
  • Expect roughly an inch of growth a year. Bucephalandra is among the slowest plants sold. The pad will look much as it does now for a long time, which is exactly why it works as a permanent feature.
  • Keep the light low. A slow plant under bright light collects algae faster than it grows new leaves. Low to medium light keeps the leaves clean and holds the blues and purples better.
  • The coconut pad will soften over time. That is normal. By the time it does, the rhizomes have knitted together and hold their own shape.

products.title: Hygrophila Kompakt
products.body_html:
Want a Hygrophila that stays in the midground? Hygrophila corymbosa 'Kompakt' is the dwarf cultivar — broad bright green oval leaves on stems with much shorter internodes, so it grows into a dense low bush instead of running for the surface like standard corymbosa.

What You’ll Receive

Your choice of Loose Fresh-Cut Plants, Fresh-Cut Bunched, or Fresh-Cut Potted

  • Loose Fresh-Cut Plants: Includes approximately 3+ loose, fresh-cut stems without roots. Perfect for flexible planting arrangements.
  • Fresh-Cut Bunched: Approximately 3+ fresh-cut stems without roots, bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.
  • Fresh-Cut Potted: About 3+ fresh-cut stems without roots, securely potted in a net pot with rockwool, ensuring stability and healthy growth.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Kompakt, also known as Compact Hygrophila
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila corymbosa 'Kompakt'
  • Also known as — Nomaphila siamensis 'Parvifolia'
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Midground
  • Shipped size — Approx. 3+ fresh-cut stems, roughly 3-6 in
  • Mature height — 4–8 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium. Stronger light keeps the internodes short and the bush tight
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed in paludariums
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops and side shoots

Grower’s Notes

  • Short internodes are the whole point. Standard Hygrophila corymbosa stretches to 20 inches and beyond with wide gaps between leaf pairs. 'Kompakt' packs them close, which is why it holds a hedge shape where the parent plant does not — and why it fits a 10-gallon tank that the parent would swamp.
  • Light keeps it compact. Under weak light the internodes lengthen and it loses the dwarf habit — trimming won't bring it back.
  • Trim and replant the tops. Each cut forces side shoots, which is how a few stems become a solid midground block.
  • Root tabs help noticeably. It draws from both roots and water column, and leaf size drops in inert gravel.
  • Also available as sterile Kompakt Vitro Culture.

  • CO₂ — Not required. It grows fuller and denser with it
  • Water — 60–75°F · pH 6.0–7.0. It prefers cooler water than most tropical stems
  • Substrate — Not required. It feeds mainly from the water column
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower's Notes

  • Keep it cool. This is a European species, not a tropical one. It performs best between 60 and 75°F and thins out in a warm discus or heavily heated tank. That makes it a useful choice for an unheated room-temperature aquarium, where most stem plants sulk.
  • Trim to build the bush. Left alone it grows as single stems. Topping triggers branching, and repeated trimming is what produces the dense feathery clusters it is bought for.
  • Rinse the gel off and separate the plantlets before planting, spacing them an inch apart. Fine whorled foliage shades itself when planted as a clump.
  • Dose the water column. It takes most of what it needs through its foliage rather than its roots.
  • The pale lime-green sits well against darker or broader-leaved plants — it reads as light rather than color, which is a different kind of contrast from a red stem.

Notes

  • Appearance, size, and coloration may vary depending on growing conditions and season. Tissue culture plants may initially appear small but will quickly establish and grow once planted in aquarium conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Hygrophila Pink Chai Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Want neon pink rather than red? Hygrophila lancea 'Pink Chai' carries vivid pink through its stems and narrow elongated leaves — a color no other stem plant in our range produces. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format, free of snails, algae and pesticide residue.

What You’ll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing multiple Hygrophila Pink Chai plantlets, ready for rinsing, acclimation, and planting.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pink Chai
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila lancea 'Pink Chai'
  • Also known as — Hygrophila sp. 'Pink Chai', Hygrophila sp. 'Chai', Hygrophila Pink Lady
  • Origin — Natural hybrid of Hygrophila lancea 'Araguaia', found at South Island Aquarium in Singapore
  • Placement — Midground
  • Shipped size — Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 in
  • Mature height — 4–10 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium. Stronger light intensifies the pink
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5. Sensitive to sudden changes
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Stability matters more than intensity. Pink Chai reacts to sudden shifts in parameters more than most Hygrophila. A steady tank produces better color than a heavily dosed one that swings.
  • Occasional stems revert. The hybrid is stable and cuttings normally come true pink, but a stem may sometimes return to the reddish-brown of the parent Hygrophila lancea 'Araguaia'. That is the hybrid behaving normally, not a mislabeled plant — remove reverted stems if you want the stand to stay uniformly pink.
  • Divide the cup into small clumps and plant them a little apart. Tissue culture stock establishes faster with space around it.
  • Rinse the gel off completely before planting or it clouds water and feeds algae in the first weeks.
  • Trim regularly and replant the tops. Topping forces branching, which is what turns a few stems into a block of color.

Prefer rooted plants? See Hygrophila Pink Chai (Small Size) or the standard size.

products.title: Anacharis
products.body_html:
New tank battling algae, or a pond that needs oxygenating? Anacharis is the workhorse. It grows fast enough to strip nitrate before algae can use it, tolerates cold water down to 60°F, and asks for nothing but light — no CO₂, no substrate, no fuss.

What You’ll Receive

You’ll receive approximately 6 fresh Anacharis stems in the format of your choice:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Loose, freshly trimmed stems
  • Bunched Plants: Fresh-cut stems bundled with foam and lead weight
  • Potted Plants: Fresh-cut stems planted in rock wool inside a net pot

All plants are submerged-grown and hand-selected for health and quality.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Anacharis, Brazilian Waterweed, Elodea
  • Scientific name — Egeria densa
  • Placement — Background, or floating as an oxygenator
  • Mature height — 12–24 in and beyond
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner. Close to unkillable in the right state
  • Light — Low to medium is plenty
  • CO₂ — Not required! It grows fast enough without
  • Water — 60–82°F · pH 6.5–8.5, and it handles hard alkaline water easily
  • Feeding — Root and water column
  • Propagation — Cuttings; snap a stem and replant it

Grower’s Notes

  • It works planted or floating. Floating stems grow fastest and strip the most nitrate, which is why it is the classic new-tank and pond plant — planting it is optional.
  • It handles cold. At 60°F it keeps growing when tropical stems stall, making it one of the few plants suited to unheated tanks and outdoor ponds.
  • Trim and replant the tops. Lower stems go bare as they age; cut the healthy top few inches and discard the base rather than waiting for it to refill.
  • Brittle on arrival is normal. Stems snap easily in transit — every fragment with a node will root and grow, so plant the pieces rather than binning them.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference; stem length and leaf density vary with lighting and growing conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Cabomba Furcata
products.body_html:
Fine, feathery whorls in pink to reddish-purple — the most delicate texture of any red stem plant, and the reason it's worth the trouble. It is genuinely demanding: high light and pressurized CO₂ are what keep it from unraveling.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as loose Fresh-cut plants, Bunched plants, or Potted plants
  • Fresh-cut plants: Approx. 6 stems, loose fresh-cut stems without root
  • Bunched plants: Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems without root, bundled with foam, and lead weight
  • Potted plants: Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems without root, potted with net pot and rockwool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Red Cabomba, Fanwort
  • Scientific name — Cabomba furcata
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — High
  • CO₂ — Required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–6.8
  • Feeding — Water column
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower’s Notes

  • This is the least forgiving red stem in common cultivation. Without strong light and pressurized CO₂ the whorls thin, the stems go bare from the bottom, and it falls apart within weeks.
  • It wants soft, acidic water. Above pH 7 it struggles regardless of how good the light and CO₂ are.
  • Plant stems individually, an inch or so apart. Bunched together they shade each other and rot in the middle.
  • Stable conditions matter more than rich ones. It sheds whorls after water changes that swing temperature or chemistry sharply.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference; color and density vary considerably with lighting, CO₂ and water chemistry.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Samolus Parviflorus Red
products.body_html:
Want red without the usual difficulty? Samolus parviflorus 'Red' forms low compact rosettes that turn deep red when grown submerged — and unlike most red plants, it does not demand pressurized CO₂ and extreme light to get there.

What You’ll Receive

Enhance your aquarium with our versatile selection of high-quality aquatic plants, available in three convenient formats:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Includes approximately 1-2 fresh-cut stems without roots. Perfect for flexible planting arrangements.
  • Fresh-Cut Bunched: Approximately 1-2 fresh-cut stems without roots, bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.
  • Fresh-Cut Potted: About 1-2 fresh-cut stems without roots, securely potted in a net pot with rockwool, ensuring stability and healthy growth.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Samolus Red, also known as Red Lettuce
  • Scientific name — Samolus parviflorus 'Red'
  • Also known as — Lysimachia parvifolia 'Red'
  • Origin — Limestone rivers of South China (Guangxi)
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 2–6 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Intensity deepens the red
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 65–78°F · pH 6.5–7.5. Prefers the cooler end
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Green emersed, red submerged
  • Propagation — Side shoots and separated rosettes

Grower’s Notes

  • It arrives green. Grown emersed the leaves are green; the red only develops once it converts to submerged growth under decent light. Judge the color after a few weeks, not on arrival.
  • It prefers cooler water than most. At 65–78°F it sits below the usual range, so it does better in a room-temperature tank than a warm one.
  • It comes from limestone rivers, so hard water is no obstacle — useful if your tap water has defeated other red plants.
  • Propagate by separating side shoots. Each rosette establishes independently, so a couple of plants become a patch over a season.
  • As a rosette it stays put rather than climbing, which makes it far easier to place than a red stem plant.

products.title: Christmas Moss
products.body_html:
Want a moss with actual structure rather than a green tangle? Christmas Moss grows in flat, triangular fronds that branch like tiny fir boughs, holding a defined shape as it fills in. It's the moss aquascapers reach for when the moss itself is meant to be seen.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a small loose portion, approx. 2" x 2" in size
  • Perfect to attached to driftwood, rock, or stone

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Christmas Moss, Xmas Moss
  • Scientific name — Vesicularia montagnei
  • Also known as — Taxiphyllum sp. 'Christmas', Vesicularia sp. 'Christmas'
  • Placement — Midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 2–4 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner to keep, though slower to establish than Java Moss
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light brings algae it grows too slowly to shed
  • CO₂ — Not required! It simply branches denser and faster with it
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Feeding — Water column
  • Propagation — Fragmentation; every trimmed piece grows on

Grower’s Notes

  • Cooler water is what produces the true Christmas shape. Above roughly 78°F the fronds grow looser and longer and it starts to look like ordinary Java Moss — the tight triangular branching is a cool-water trait.
  • Tie it on thin and let it thicken. A thick pad shades and rots underneath long before the surface fills in, and Christmas Moss is too slow to recover from that quickly.
  • Trim the surface every few weeks once established. Cutting forces branching, which is what keeps the frond shape crisp instead of stringy.
  • Gentle flow keeps it clean. The dense fronds trap detritus in still water, and a silted moss browns from the inside out.

Looking to buy in bulk? Get 10 or 20 portions in one order with our Christmas Moss Bulk Pack and save 40–50% per portion.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Aquarium Moss Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference. Portion shape, density and frond form vary with temperature and growing conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Hornwort
products.body_html:
Want a plant that fights algae for you? Hornwort grows without roots, floating or tucked into decor, and strips nutrients from the water fast enough to starve algae out. It also releases compounds that suppress algae directly — one of very few aquarium plants that does.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as loose fresh-cut plants:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual, loose-cut stems without root

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Hornwort, Coontail
  • Scientific name — Ceratophyllum demersum
  • Placement — Floating or background
  • Mature height — 10–20 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 64–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. It has no roots and feeds entirely from the water column
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic. Cannot be grown emersed
  • Propagation — Stem cuttings

Grower’s Notes

  • It has no roots and never will. Those pale threads are modified leaves, not roots — planting the base in substrate just rots it. Let it float, or wedge a stem between rocks or wood to anchor it.
  • Expect needle drop on arrival and after any big change. Hornwort sheds when conditions shift and regrows within a week or two. The mess is temporary; keep the firm green stems.
  • It tolerates cold. Comfortable from 64°F, which makes it one of the few plants that works in an unheated tank, a goldfish tank or a pond.
  • Trim and replant tops, discard bare stems. Like most fast stems, the lower section goes bare and does not refoliate.
  • It grows fast enough to shade everything below. Thin it every week or two rather than letting the mat close over.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Hornwort Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference. Hornwort is a delicate, rootless plant and may shed some needles during shipping or after introduction — this is normal and it will regrow quickly under stable conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Echinodorus Red Flame
products.body_html:
Red without a red stem plant. Echinodorus 'Red Flame' carries broad green leaves scattered with bold red speckling and mottling — color that arrives as pattern rather than a solid block, and on a sturdy rosette plant that needs no trimming regime to keep it. Where red stems demand constant topping, a sword just sits there and holds the color.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose bare-root plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 1–2 individual bare-root plants
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 1–2 plants bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 1–2 plants rooted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Red Flame Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus 'Red Flame'
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 10–16 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Light intensity sets how strongly the red speckling shows
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — nutrient substrate and root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on flower stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Feed it at the roots or don't bother. Swords pull most of their nutrition from the substrate. Liquid dosing alone gives you a pale, stalled plant; root tabs under the crown give you the speckling.
  • Expect the first leaves to melt. Nursery plants grow emersed, and the emersed leaves die back after planting. The second flush is the one that shows the pattern.
  • Plant the crown at substrate level. Burying it rots the plant.
  • It propagates from flower stalks, not runners. A mature plant sends up an inflorescence carrying plantlets along its length. Let each root and grow three or four leaves, then cut it free and plant it separately.
  • Give it room. At 10–16 inches with broad leaves, one plant will shade a surprising area, so treat it as a focal point rather than a filler.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Amazon Sword (Echinodorus) Care Guide.

Notes

  • Color intensity will vary depending on light, nutrients, and water conditions. Older leaves may melt after planting; new growth will adapt to aquarium conditions.

products.title: Cryptocoryne Undulatus Red Vitro Culture

Wavy edges, bronze-red leaves. Cryptocoryne undulatus 'Red' — the wavy leaf crypt — grows narrow, strongly undulating leaves that color reddish to bronze under decent light and nutrients. Movement in the leaf edge plus warm color, on a plant that asks for neither CO₂ nor strong lighting. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne undulatus 'Red'

Care
