products.title: Dwarf Hairgrass | Bulk Pack
products.body_html:
A carpet is built from many small clumps, not a few large ones. Dwarf Hairgrass spreads by runner into a fine, meadow-like lawn — the classic Iwagumi foreground — and this bulk pack gives you 10, 20 or 30 clumps at volume pricing, enough to plant a full foreground in one session instead of waiting months for a single portion to travel across it.

You may know it as Eleocharis parvula. That is the trade name — see the note below.

What You'll Receive

Fresh, healthy Dwarf Hairgrass cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®.

Each portion consists of approximately one small clump measuring about 1" x 1" inches.

10 Pack: 10 individual small clumps (approximately 1" x 1" each)

20 Pack: 20 individual small clumps (approximately 1" x 1" each)

30 Pack: 30 individual small clumps (approximately 1" x 1" each)

For best results, separate each clump into smaller portions and plant them a short distance apart to encourage faster carpet formation.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Dwarf Hairgrass
  • Scientific name — Eleocharis pusilla
  • Also known as — Eleocharis parvula (misapplied trade name)
  • Origin — Australia and New Zealand
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Shipped size — 10 to 30 clumps, each approx. 1" x 1"
  • Mature height — 3–6 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Why two scientific names?

Dwarf Hairgrass has been sold as Eleocharis parvula in the aquarium trade for a very long time, and most hobbyists still know it by that name.

Eleocharis parvula is a real species — but it is a brackish water plant, not suited to freshwater aquariums. Almost everything sold in the hobby under that label is in fact Eleocharis pusilla, a freshwater species.

So the plant you receive is Eleocharis pusilla: the same Dwarf Hairgrass you have always bought, correctly named, and genuinely suited to a freshwater tank.

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Light must reach the substrate for it to carpet rather than stretch
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Dry start works well
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower's Notes

  • Separate every clump before planting. Divide each clump into smaller portions and set them a short distance apart. Spread out, they close ranks faster than an intact clump would spread on its own, because runners only travel into open substrate.
  • Keeping it alive is easy; carpeting it is not. That gap is why this is rated Intermediate. Survival needs little, but a dense low lawn needs strong light at substrate level and usually CO₂ — without both, expect a thin, stretched meadow.
  • Trim the carpet once established. Cutting it back triggers a flush of runners and thickens the mat rather than adding height.
  • Feed at the roots. Runner production stalls without a nutrient substrate or root tabs, and that is what decides how quickly the gaps close.
  • Expect the emersed blades to melt back in the first weeks. New growth comes from the runners, not the original blades — leave it alone through the transition.

Want a shorter, flatter lawn? The Dwarf Hairgrass Mini Bulk Pack stays 1–2 in. Just need one portion? See the standard Dwarf Hairgrass, or the sterile Vitro Culture format.

products.title: Brazilian Pennywort
products.body_html:
Want one plant you can use three ways? Brazilian Pennywort grows planted in substrate, draped over hardscape, or left floating at the surface — and it does all three well. Round coin-shaped leaves on creeping stems, growing fast enough to fill a gap in weeks.

What You’ll Receive

Fresh, healthy Brazilian Pennywort cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in convenient planting formats:

Fresh Cut Plants: Approximately 4 fresh-cut stems without roots.
Fresh Cut Bunched: Approximately 4 stems bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.
Fresh Cut Potted: About 4 stems potted securely in a net pot with rockwool for stability and easy planting.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Brazilian Pennywort
  • Scientific name — Hydrocotyle leucocephala
  • Placement — Midground, or floating
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required if planted; none needed if floated
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Runners and stem cuttings

Grower’s Notes

  • Floating is a legitimate way to grow it, not a failure. Left at the surface it grows faster, throws roots into the water column and shades the tank below — useful in a shrimp or fry tank. Planted, it grows more upright and compact. Both are correct; choose deliberately.
  • It responds strongly to trimming. Every cut forces branching, which is how a few stems become a bush — and how you keep a fast plant from taking the tank.
  • It strips nitrate quickly, which makes it genuinely useful in a newly cycled or heavily stocked tank.
  • Replant the trimmed tops. Cut stems root within days whether planted or floated.

products.title: Cryptocoryne Balansae Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Cryptocoryne balansae grows like Vallisneria and behaves like a crypt. Long ribbon leaves with a deeply hammered, puckered surface rise a foot or more and sway with the flow — all without CO₂ or strong lighting. It is the low-tech route to a moving green background.

What You'll Receive

  • One (1) Vitro Culture® 4-inch bag of Cryptocoryne crispatula var. balansae
  • Yield: Approximately 3–4 young plantlets, ready to plant into your aquascape

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Balansae Crypt
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne crispatula var. balansae
  • Also known as — Crypt Balansae, Cryptocoryne balansae
  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Background
  • Mature height — 12-20 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; this is a root feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower's Notes

  • It handles hard, alkaline water better than most crypts. Balansae comes from limestone streams, so it suits tap water that other Cryptocoryne sulk in — a genuinely useful trait if your water is hard.
  • Expect melt, then ribbon leaves. Tissue culture plantlets shed their emersed foliage as they convert. Leave the roots undisturbed; the long submersed leaves start appearing within three to six weeks.
  • The hammered texture develops with age. Young leaves come out relatively smooth. The puckered, quilted surface — the reason to buy this over Vallisneria — shows on mature growth.
  • Root tabs, not liquid dosing. A 12-20 inch leaf takes a lot of energy and crypts draw it from the substrate. Enriched soil or tabs under the crown are what produce full-length leaves.
  • Plant the crown at substrate level and then leave it. Bury the roots only. Every replant restarts the melt cycle, so choose the position before planting and let the runners spread on their own.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Cryptocoryne Care Guide.

Notes

  • Pictures shown are for reference only. Actual plant size, shape, and color may vary depending on growing conditions. This Vitro Culture® bag is sealed for freshness—please follow proper sterilization and acclimation procedures upon opening.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Cryptocoryne Balansae
products.body_html:
Want the look of Vallisneria from a Crypt? Cryptocoryne crispatula var. balansae sends up long, narrow ribbon leaves with a distinctive hammered, ruffled texture — a background plant that moves like grass but behaves like a Crypt, and one that takes hard water in its stride.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as Bare-root Plants, Bunched Plants, or Potted Plants
  • Bare-root plants | approx. 1-2 plants loose, bare-root portion
  • Bunched plants | approx. 1-2 plants bundled with foam, and lead weight
  • Potted plants | approx. 1-2 plants with net pot and rock wool
  • Young plants grow in a controlled laboratory environment

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Balansae Crypt
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne crispatula var. balansae
  • Also known as — Cryptocoryne balansae
  • Origin — Southern Thailand
  • Placement — Background
  • Mature height — 12–20 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Brighter light brings bronze tones into the leaves
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5. Hard water with good calcium suits it well
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Hard water is not a problem here. Cryptocoryne generally do well in harder water than most planted-tank species, and balansae is no exception — it appreciates a good calcium content. If your tap water is hard and stem plants have disappointed you, Crypts are the group to look at.
  • Expect it to melt after planting. Crypts drop their leaves on a change of conditions and rebuild from the roots over two to four weeks. Leave it alone through that.
  • Feed at the roots and place it once. Crypts melt again every time they are moved, so decide position before planting.
  • Slow to start, then quick. Once established it spreads by runner and fills a background with little further help.
  • Leaf color ranges from lush green to bronze depending on light — both are healthy.

products.title: Pogostemon Deccanensis Vitro Culture (Pogostemon Erectus)
products.body_html:
Miniature conifers in a planted tank. Pogostemon deccanensis — the Indian Star plant — packs fine needle-like leaves densely around upright stems, giving vertical structure no broad-leaved plant can. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format: pest-free, algae-free and pesticide-free.

What You’ll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing multiple healthy Pogostemon deccanensis plantlets—ready to rinse, acclimate, and plant in your aquarium.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pogostemon Erectus
  • Scientific name — Pogostemon deccanensis
  • Also known as — Pogostemon erectus, Indian Star
  • Origin — Maharashtra, western India
  • Placement — Background, in groups
  • Shipped size — Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 in
  • Mature height — 10–20 in
  • Suits — 20 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Strong light keeps it compact rather than stretched
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Vigorous rooter — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Grown emersed it produces violet flower spikes
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Why two names? The hobby sold this as Pogostemon erectus for years before it was correctly identified as P. deccanensis. Same plant, both labels still in use.
  • Divide the portion into small clumps of a few plantlets and plant them an inch apart rather than as one mass. They fill in faster that way.
  • Rinse the gel off completely before planting or it clouds water and feeds algae in the first weeks.
  • Yellowing or melt in the first weeks is the emersed-to-submerged conversion, not a failure. Keep light and CO₂ steady.

products.title: Anubias Coffeefolia
products.body_html:
Want texture from an Anubias? Coffeefolia grows deeply rippled, corrugated leaves that look closer to a coffee plant than a typical smooth Anubias — and new leaves emerge bronze-copper before hardening to deep green, so an actively growing plant shows both colors at once.

What You’ll Receive

  • Bare-Root Plants: One Anubias Coffeefolia plant with 4 or more healthy leaves, loose and unpotted
  • Potted Plants: One Anubias Coffeefolia plant with 4 or more healthy leaves, rooted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Coffeefolia Anubias
  • Scientific name — Anubias barteri 'Coffeefolia'
  • Placement — Midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 6–10 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner. As tough as any Anubias
  • Light — Low to medium. Shade suits it; bright light means algae on slow leaves
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower’s Notes

  • The bronze is new growth, not stress. Fresh leaves come in coppery-bronze and darken to green over several weeks. A plant showing bronze at the growing tip is a healthy plant, not a deficient one.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots can go into substrate; the rhizome cannot. Buried, it rots — the most common way an Anubias is lost.
  • The rippled surface traps detritus more than a smooth leaf does. A gentle wave of the hand during water changes keeps it clean.
  • Keep it shaded. Slow growth means algae settles faster than the plant replaces the leaf, and textured leaves are harder to wipe.
  • Divide with a clean blade, keeping at least three leaves per section.

products.title: Bucephalandra Kedagang Blue Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Kedagang Blue, also sold as Buce Godzilla Blue, carries dark green leaves with a blue cast that deepens once the plant settles into submersed growth. Kedagang is the plant; Godzilla is the trade name, and color is what separates one Kedagang from another.

What You'll Receive

  • One sealed 4-inch Vitro Culture® tissue culture bag
  • Approximately 4 small plantlets grown in sterile nutrient gel
  • 100% free from snails, algae, pesticides and pathogens
  • Rinse the gel away and separate the plantlets before planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Kedagang Blue Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Kedagang Blue'
  • Also known as — Buce Godzilla Blue, Bucephalandra Blue Godzilla
  • Origin — Borneo (genus range)
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Too much light brings algae the plant is too slow to outgrow.
  • CO₂ — Not required. Deepens color and speeds growth if you already run it.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed. Epiphyte; attaches to wood or rock.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rhizome creeper; grows submersed or emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Your light source decides whether this plant looks blue. The blue is a surface reflection rather than a pigment. Under RGB or full-spectrum lighting it reads clearly blue-green; under warm white the same plant looks dark green. Check the light before assuming you received the wrong thing.
  • Godzilla means Kedagang. The Godzilla name travels with several Kedagang color forms — blue, red, pink. Same plant type; buy on the color you want rather than the name.
  • Rinse the gel off completely and separate the four plantlets before attaching. Leftover nutrient agar clouds water and feeds algae.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie it to wood or rock and leave it exposed; buried rhizomes rot.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.

products.title: Aponogeton Longiplumulosus
products.body_html:
Deeply ruffled leaves that move with the current. Aponogeton longiplumulosus is a Madagascar bulb plant that grows long, flowing, heavily undulating leaves — the ruffling is pronounced enough that the plant reads as movement rather than mass. It grows fast and wants room; 20 gallons is a sensible minimum.

What You'll Receive

At Aquarium Plants Factory®, we offer two options to suit every aquarist's preference:

  • Sprouted Bulb With Leaf – A healthy bulb that has already sprouted and includes at least one leaf for a guaranteed head start
  • Bulb Only Without Leaf – A healthy dormant bulb for experienced hobbyists who prefer to grow the plant from its resting stage

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Ruffled Aponogeton
  • Scientific name — Aponogeton longiplumulosus
  • Family — Aponogetonaceae
  • Origin — Madagascar
  • Plant type — Bulb / tuber
  • Placement — Midground to background; best in larger aquariums
  • Suits — 20 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Optional but beneficial
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — True aquatic. Cannot be grown emersed
  • Propagation — Bulb division

Grower's Notes

  • Give it 20 gallons or leave it alone. Fast growth and long ruffled leaves mean a single bulb dominates a small tank within weeks. In a nano it is not a centerpiece, it is the whole scape.
  • Set the bulb on the substrate, don't bury it. Leave the top third exposed; buried bulbs rot instead of sprouting.
  • A dormant rest is normal. Leaves die back, the bulb rests, and growth resumes. Leave it in place rather than discarding it.
  • Root tabs are not optional on a fast-growing bulb plant. It exhausts its own reserves and then stalls in inert gravel.
  • The ruffling shows best with some water movement. In dead-still water the leaves hang rather than flow, which loses most of the effect.

Notes

  • Bulbs without leaves are healthy and capable of sprouting under proper aquarium conditions. Sprouting time varies depending on water parameters, lighting, and aquarium stability. If you're new to bulb plants or prefer immediate results, we strongly recommend selecting the Sprouted Bulb With Leaf option.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Samolus Valerandi

Miniature lettuce, underwater. It grows submerged in an aquarium or emersed in a paludarium or riparium equally well.

products.title: Dwarf Baby Tears
products.body_html:
The finest carpet in the hobby, and the least forgiving. Dwarf Baby Tears — HC Cuba — has leaves a few millimeters across, so a healthy carpet reads at a scale nothing else matches. It also wants high light, CO₂, and water below 78°F. Get those right and it carpets fast; get them wrong and it lifts off the substrate in sheets.

What You’ll Receive

Select the format that best fits your aquascape:

  • Fresh-cut Plants
    Small loose clusters of HC (approx. 1"x1"), ideal for immediate planting and the most efficient way to establish a healthy HC carpet.
  • Rooted Bunched Plants
    Healthy stems tied with weight for quick anchoring and faster establishment.
  • Rooted Potted Plants
    Fully rooted plants grown in rockwool — the easiest to transition and quickest to carpet.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Dwarf Baby Tears, HC Cuba
  • Scientific name — Micranthemum callitrichoides 'Cuba'
  • Also known as — Hemianthus callitrichoides 'Cuba' (the older name, still in wide use), HC Cuba, HC
  • Origin — Cuba
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Shipped size — Small clusters approx. 1"x1", or rooted portions
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Suits — 5 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast, once established

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — High. Light must reach the substrate, not just the surface
  • CO₂ — Required
  • Water — 68–78°F · pH 6.0–7.0. Note the ceiling — HC struggles in warm tanks
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich soil
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Runners and stolons

Grower’s Notes

  • Temperature is the overlooked failure. People blame light and CO₂ when a carpet melts, but HC does poorly above about 78°F. In a tank running at 80–82°F for discus or similar, it will not hold — use Monte Carlo instead.
  • Two names, one plant. Most of the hobby knows it as Hemianthus callitrichoides; the accepted name is now Micranthemum callitrichoides. You will see both on shop shelves and in forums.
  • Plant small — three or four leaves per portion, half an inch apart. Large clumps rot in the middle and float off.
  • A carpet that lifts is a rooting problem, not a nutrient problem. Press portions firmly into fine substrate and keep flow off them until they anchor.
  • If this sounds like more than you want, Micranthemum Monte Carlo carpets in similar style with far less demand.

products.title: Bacopa Australis
products.body_html:
Want bright green in a tank full of dark plants? Bacopa australis is one of the lightest greens available — small rounded leaves in tight pairs up a fast, bushy stem. It reads almost lime against Anubias and Crypts, which is what makes it useful.

products.title: Microsorum Trident Mini
products.body_html:
Trident Java Fern, at nano scale. Leptochilus pteropus 'Trident Mini' keeps the narrow forked leaf that gives Trident its name — each blade splitting into finger-like lobes — but stops at 2–4 inches instead of 8 or more. In a small tank that difference is what makes it usable.

products.title: Microsorum Pteropus 'Needle'
products.body_html:
The finest leaf in the Java Fern range. Microsorum pteropus 'Needle' grows long, narrow, sharply pointed blades — thinner again than Narrow Leaf, so a mature plant reads as a spray of dark green lines rather than a mass of foliage. Same indestructible fern underneath.

  • Common name — Needle Java Fern

  • Black spots on older leaves are usually plantlets forming, not disease. Let them grow a few leaves and roots, then detach and attach them elsewhere.

products.title: Echinodorus Chocolate Marble
products.body_html:
A sword with markings, not just color. Echinodorus 'Chocolate Marble' carries a heavy blotched pattern across its leaves — irregular dark mottling on green, closer to camouflage than to the even tones most swords show. It grows to full sword size, so it needs a tank with room.

What You'll Receive

  • Difficulty — Beginner

  • Root tabs are the whole game with swords. Chocolate Marble takes almost everything it needs from the substrate. In inert gravel with liquid dosing alone it stalls and the marbling fades — which people mistake for a difficult plant rather than a hungry one.

  • Plant the crown at substrate level, never below — buried crowns rot.
  • Expect the first leaves to melt as it converts from emersed nursery growth. The second flush shows the real pattern.

products.body_html:
Milfoil in pale gold instead of green. Myriophyllum mattogrossense 'Golden' carries the same fine feathered whorls as the standard species, but under strong light the foliage runs very pale yellow to nearly white, sometimes with reddish tips. It is a striking plant and a demanding one — the color comes from low pigment, which makes it slow to recover and quick to show algae.

  • Pack 5 — 5 × 4-inch Vitro Culture® bags, each yielding many small plantlets
  • Pack 10 — 10 × 4-inch Vitro Culture® bags, for larger aquascaping projects

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Golden Mattogrossense Milfoil
  • Scientific name — Myriophyllum mattogrossense 'Golden'
  • Also known as — Golden Watermilfoil, White Milfoil
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Brazil
  • Placement — Midground to background

  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate

  • CO₂ — Recommended. Pale foliage photosynthesizes less, so carbon matters more here than on the green form
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.0
  • Substrate — Optional. It feeds mainly from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Grown emersed in the lab, converts to submerged growth in your tank
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Put it in a mature tank, not a new one. This is the single thing that decides whether it works. Pale leaves carry little chlorophyll, so the plant cannot outgrow algae — and algae settling on golden foliage destroys the color you bought it for. A stable, established tank with good algae control is close to a requirement.
  • Light decides the color. Strong lighting gives pale gold to near-white with reddish tips; weaker light gives ordinary green.
  • Plant stems individually an inch apart. Fine whorls shade each other badly when a bunch goes in as one lump.
  • Trim and replant the tops. It branches readily from below the cut, and repeated topping builds a dense group.
  • Pair it against dark green or red planting — the contrast is most of the effect. The standard green Mattogrossense is far more forgiving if you want the texture without the difficulty.

Why two scientific names?

Dwarf Hairgrass has been sold as Eleocharis parvula in the aquarium trade for a very long time, and most hobbyists still know it by that name.

Eleocharis parvula is a real species — but it is a brackish water plant, not suited to freshwater aquariums. Almost everything sold in the hobby under that label is in fact Eleocharis pusilla, a freshwater species.

So the plant you receive is Eleocharis pusilla: the same Dwarf Hairgrass you have always bought, correctly named, and genuinely suited to a freshwater tank.

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Light must reach the substrate for it to carpet
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required

Grower’s Notes

  • Divide the cup into many small portions. Plant groups of a few blades an inch apart. Runners only travel into open substrate, so a single lump takes months longer to fill a foreground than the same plant spread out.
  • Keeping it alive is easy; carpeting it is not. That gap is why this is rated Intermediate. Survival needs little, but a dense low lawn needs strong light at substrate level and usually CO₂.

products.title: Utricularia Graminifolia Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Want the softest carpet in aquascaping? Utricularia graminifolia — UG — forms a fine, bright green lawn with a fluffy texture nothing else matches. It is also a bladderwort, a carnivorous plant, though its traps are microscopic and target single-celled organisms. It is safe with fish and shrimp, including newborn shrimplets.

What You’ll Receive

One Vitro Culture® portion of Utricularia graminifolia

  • Sold as a 4-inch sealed bag or a 2.5-inch cup, depending on availability (customer cannot choose).
  • Lab-grown in sterile gel/liquid, free from snails, algae, pathogens, and pesticides.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — UG, Grass-leaved Bladderwort
  • Scientific name — Utricularia graminifolia
  • Family — Lentibulariaceae (bladderworts)
  • Placement — Foreground carpet
  • Mature height — 0.5–1 in
  • Growth rate — Fast once established

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — High
  • CO₂ — Required
  • Water — 68–78°F · pH 6.0–7.0. Soft water suits it best
  • Substrate — Required. Fine-grain nutrient soil
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Dry start works well
  • Propagation — Stolons

Grower’s Notes

  • Establishment is the hard part, not maintenance. UG commonly melts in the first two to three weeks while it converts from emersed tissue culture growth. Once it has taken hold it grows quickly and needs little from you. Most losses happen in that first month.
  • Stability matters more than any single value. UG reacts badly to swinging CO₂, temperature or hardness — a steady tank beats a heavily dosed one.
  • The dry start method is the most reliable route. Plant into damp soil, cover to hold humidity, and let it carpet emersed for four to six weeks before flooding slowly.
  • Press small clumps into fine substrate rather than planting deep. UG has no real roots — it anchors with fine stolons, which is also why an established mat can lift in sheets if left untrimmed.
  • Carnivorous but harmless. The bladders are a fraction of a millimeter across and catch protozoa and rotifers. Shrimp keepers use UG routinely in breeding tanks.

New to sterile cups? Read our guide on preparing tissue culture plants, or compare options in our Best Carpet Plants guide.

Notes

  • Utricularia graminifolia can be a challenging plant for beginners, as it requires stable water parameters, CO₂, and strong lighting for best results. Pictures are for reference only — plants may vary in size, shape, and color depending on growing conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

  • It is a stem plant pretending to be a rosette. Under good light it stays compact and reads as a foreground cluster. Let the light drop and it reverts to stretching upward like its full-size parent — at which point it is no longer a foreground plant.

products.body_html:

Be aware before buying: despite Cryptocoryne being an easy genus in general, this cultivar is genuinely difficult. It is sensitive to unstable conditions and is not a beginner plant.

  • Difficulty — Advanced

products.body_html:
Most red stem plants demand high light, injected CO₂ and a soft-water tank before they show any color at all. Rotala 'Wayanad' is easier than that. It colors from green through orange under medium-high light, and the narrow lance-shaped leaves give a finer texture than the round-leaved macrandra types — closer to rotundifolia in habit, but with warmer tones.

What You'll Receive

Plant Profile

  • Common name: Rotala Wayanad

  • Placement: Midground to background
  • Shipped size: Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 inches

  • Difficulty: Intermediate
  • Light: Medium to high. It grows green under medium light and shifts toward orange and red as intensity rises.
  • CO₂: Recommended. Injection tightens the node spacing and deepens the color; without it the stems grow leggier and stay green.
  • Water: pH 6.0-7.5, 72-82°F (22-28°C)

  • Trim it hard and often. Fast growth is only useful if you use it. Cutting the group back by a third every couple of weeks forces side shoots and builds the dense bush this plant is capable of.

products.body_html:
Kedagang Red is one of the more strongly colored Bucephalandra — deep green leaves that flush red-bronze under the right light, on a compact rhizome. This one arrives already grown onto a rock, so there is no tying and no waiting for it to grip.

What You'll Receive

  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Kedagang Red'

products.title: Bucephalandra Red Sword
products.body_html:
A Bucephalandra with a sword leaf. Bucephalandra sp. 'Sekadau Red Sword' grows narrow, elongated, pointed leaves that develop ruffled margins as the plant reaches adult size — a shape almost nothing else in the genus offers. Mature foliage is dark green to olive-brown; the red and pink sit on new growth and leaf undersides, where strong light brings them out.

What You'll Receive

Sold in three formats — choose at checkout:

  • Bare-root Plants: Loose plants with the rhizome and roots exposed, ready to tie onto hardscape with cotton thread
  • Rooted Bunched: Established plants bundled together
  • Rooted Potted: Grown on in a pot, ready to divide or mount

These pest-free, young plants were grown in a lab before transitioning ex-vitro for maximum hardiness. Expect natural variations in their initial size and color as they settle in and mature in your tank!

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Red Sword Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Sekadau Red Sword'
  • Also known as — Sekadau Red Sword, Buce, Bucep
  • Origin — Fast-flowing streams of Borneo
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 3–5 in
  • Suits — 5 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium grows the plant. Strong light brings the red into new growth and undersides
  • CO₂ — Not required. It improves color and pace, nothing more
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed — suits paludariums and Wabi-Kusa
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • This is not a solid red plant. Adult leaves are dark green to olive-brown. The rich red and pink show on new growth and on the undersides, and only when the light is strong. Under low light it still grows well — it just stays green.
  • The sword shape arrives with maturity. Young plants look like ordinary narrow-leaved Buce. The elongated, pointed leaf and its ruffled margin develop as the plant reaches its adult 3–5 inches, which takes months.
  • Tie it on with cotton thread — never glue it. Never bury the rhizome either; buried, it rots. Wrap it onto wood or stone with cotton thread and let the plant grip on its own. There is no such thing as aquarium-safe glue — it is all cyanoacrylate gel, and whatever tissue it touches burns and dies. On a rhizome that is fatal, because a rhizome does not regrow. If you have no choice, a tiny dab on the roots only, where the damage can melt away and grow back.
  • Strong light is a trade-off. It is what pulls the red into the new leaves, but Buce grows too slowly to outpace algae, so a bright position needs grazers, steady nutrients and a watchful eye on the older leaves.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.

Prefer the sterile tissue culture format? See Bucephalandra Red Sword Vitro Culture.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Bucephalandra Care Guide.

  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

  • This is not a solid red plant. Adult leaves are dark green to olive-brown. The rich red and pink show on new growth and on the undersides, and only when the light is strong. Under low light it still grows well — it just stays green.
  • The leaf shape is the reason to buy this one. Narrow, pointed and slightly wavy at the edges once mature, it reads differently in a scape from the rounded Buce sitting beside it.
  • Tie it on with cotton thread — never glue it. Never bury the rhizome either; buried, it rots. Wrap it onto wood or stone with cotton thread and let the plant grip on its own. There is no such thing as aquarium-safe glue — it is all cyanoacrylate gel, and whatever tissue it touches burns and dies. On a rhizome that is fatal, because a rhizome does not regrow. If you have no choice, a tiny dab on the roots only, where the damage can melt away and grow back.

products.title: Monosolenium Tenerum (Pellia)
products.body_html:
Thicker than moss, and that is the point. Monosolenium tenerum — Pellia — is a liverwort that grows broad ribbon-like fronds rather than fine filaments, forming dense dark green cushions with real substance. It gives a texture nothing else in a planted tank offers, and it does it in low light with no CO₂.

What You’ll Receive

  • Loose Portion: small portion of Monosolenium tenerum, approx. 2" x 2" (5 cm x 5 cm)
  • Ready for Use: Can be tied to rocks, tucked into crevices, or allowed to carpet over time

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pellia
  • Scientific name — Monosolenium tenerum
  • Also known as — Pellia Moss, Round Pellia
  • Origin — East Asia
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on rock or wood
  • Shipped size — Loose portion, approx. 2" x 2"
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Suits — 5 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light mostly feeds algae on a plant this slow
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic. Does not grow emersed
  • Propagation — Fragmentation — split a cushion and re-tie the pieces

Grower’s Notes

  • It has no roots and no grip — you must tie it down. Unlike Java Moss, Pellia is brittle and heavy and will not attach itself. Use thread, hairnet or mesh over rock, and expect to leave it several months before it holds. Dropped loose on the substrate it simply drifts apart.
  • Keep the light modest. Slow growth means algae settles faster than the plant replaces tissue, and algae inside a dense Pellia cushion cannot be cleaned out.
  • Give it flow. Water moving through the cushion keeps detritus from packing into the center and rotting.
  • Split and re-tie rather than trimming. Fragments grow into new cushions, so one portion becomes several over a year.
  • Shrimp and fry take shelter in it readily — the dense structure is better cover than fine mosses provide.

products.title: Azolla (Fairy Moss)
products.body_html:
Want surface cover that works as a nutrient sponge? Azolla is a floating fern with tiny overlapping leaves that form a soft mat across the water. It shades out algae, strips nitrate fast, and turns red or bronze under strong light or cool weather.

What You’ll Receive

Our Azolla is sold by portion size and packed in resealable bags. The dimensions below refer to the approximate bag size, not the coverage area after the plants are released into your aquarium or pond.

Portion Size Approx. Bag Size Suggested Count Notes
Small 2" × 2" 20+ Great starter portion for nano aquariums and small ponds.
Medium 3" × 3" 80+ Ideal for medium aquariums and water gardens.
Large 4" × 4" 320+ Best value for large aquariums, ponds, and rapid propagation.

Please Note:

  • Plant counts are approximate since Azolla plants naturally vary in size.
  • Azolla is extremely small and reproduces rapidly under suitable growing conditions, so the number of plants will increase over time.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Fairy Moss, Water Fern, Mosquito Fern
  • Scientific name — Azolla caroliniana
  • Placement — Floating
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium to high. Strong light is what turns it red
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 65–85°F · pH 5.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Feeds entirely from the water column
  • Propagation — Fragmentation

Grower’s Notes

  • Keep the surface calm. Azolla will not tolerate strong agitation or spray — water sitting on the fronds rots them. Aim filter outflow below the surface or fence the plants off from the turbulence.
  • Thin it weekly. It doubles quickly and a closed mat shades everything below, including your other plants. Scoop out a third at a time.
  • Red color comes from bright light and cool water, not fertilizer. In a dim warm tank it stays green.
  • It fixes nitrogen through a symbiotic cyanobacterium in its leaves, which is why it grows so fast in water most plants find lean.

products.title: Dracaena Sanderiana – Lucky Bamboo
products.body_html:
🎋 Dracaena sanderiana – Lucky Bamboo
Semi-Aquatic Ornamental Plant | Can Grow in Aquariums with Emerged Foliage

Dracaena sanderiana, widely known as Lucky Bamboo, is a beautiful and resilient ornamental plant often used in aquariums, paludariums, and indoor decorative displays. Despite its common name, Lucky Bamboo is not a true bamboo but a member of the Dracaena family. Its smooth green stems and elegant narrow leaves create a clean, minimal aesthetic that pairs beautifully with modern aquascapes and indoor plant arrangements.

One unique feature of Dracaena sanderiana is that the stem can safely grow in aquarium water, making it popular for aquarists who want a plant that bridges both aquatic and terrestrial environments. The stems tolerate full submersion, but the leaves are not adapted for underwater life.

When fully submerged, the leaves will typically decline and melt after a short period of time. For long-term health, the leaves should grow above the water line, where they will continue to develop normally and can thrive permanently in that position. This makes Lucky Bamboo ideal for aquariums where the stem is placed in water while the foliage grows above the tank.

🌟 Key Features

Scientific Name: Dracaena sanderiana
Common Name: Lucky Bamboo
Plant Type: Semi-aquatic ornamental houseplant

• Aquarium Compatible Stem: The stem can grow submerged in aquarium water.
• Emergent Growth Habit: Leaves must grow above the water surface for long-term health.
• Elegant Upright Structure: Smooth green stalks with narrow pointed leaves create a clean decorative look.
• Versatile Placement: Perfect for aquariums, paludariums, ripariums, and indoor plant displays.

🌱 Growth & Care

Lighting: Low to moderate light
Water Parameters: Adaptable to most aquarium conditions
Placement: Stem can be placed underwater, but leaves must remain above water
Growth Form: Upright stem plant with emergent foliage

Important:
While the stem tolerates submersion, the leaves will only survive a short time underwater. For permanent growth in an aquarium environment, position the plant so that the foliage grows above the water line.

🪴 Aquarium & Decorative Benefits

• Natural Aquascape Accent: Adds vertical structure and a natural look to aquariums.
• Perfect for Open-Top Tanks: Ideal for aquariums where plants can grow above the water surface.
• Low Maintenance: Hardy and adaptable, making it suitable for beginners and experienced hobbyists alike.

📦 What You’ll Receive

Fresh, healthy Dracaena sanderiana (Lucky Bamboo) carefully prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®:

Fresh Cut Plant:
• 1 healthy stem cutting approximately 8–12 inches tall with attached leaves.

⚠️ Care Disclaimer

Dracaena sanderiana is commonly used in aquariums, but only the stem should remain submerged.
Leaves are not aquatic and will not survive permanently underwater.

For best long-term results, position the plant so the stem grows in water while the leaves grow above the aquarium.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Cardamine
  • Scientific name — Cardamine lyrata
  • Also known as — Japanese Cress, Chinese Ivy
  • Origin — East Asia
  • Placement — Midground; also trails over hardscape
  • Mature height — 4–10 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 65–75°F · pH 6.5–7.5. Note the ceiling — this is a cool-water species
  • Substrate — Not required, though a nutrient substrate gives fuller growth
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed in humid terrariums
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem sections

Grower’s Notes

  • Keep it under 75°F. Cardamine comes from temperate East Asia and thins out badly in a warm tropical tank. It suits room-temperature, lightly heated and coldwater setups — which is where most of its competition won't grow.
  • Train it rather than plant it. Laid across wood or stone the stems creep and root as they go, giving a draped effect no upright stem plant produces.
  • It arrives in emersed nursery form with round leaves. Submerged growth comes in a slightly different shape — that's the plant adapting, not a mislabel.
  • Trim and replant cuttings; sections root readily from any node.
  • Fast growth means regular trimming, or it reaches the surface and shades what's below.

Notes

  • Cardamine lyrata ships in its emersed nursery form with round leaves. Once submerged, leaf shape may change and adapt to aquarium conditions. Some initial melting or leaf loss may occur during transition but new submerged growth will follow.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Rotala Rotundifolia
products.body_html:
The Rotala to start with. Rotala rotundifolia grows small round leaves in opposite pairs on fast, upright stems, and shifts from bright green to a pink or reddish tone under strong light. It's the most forgiving plant in a genus with a reputation for being demanding — and it grows fast enough to fill a background in weeks.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as an emerged loose Fresh-cut plants, Bunched plants, or Potted plants
  • Fresh-cut plants | Approx. 6 stems, loose fresh-cut stems without root
  • Bunched plants | Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems without root, bundled with foam, and lead weight
  • Potted plants | Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems without root, potted with net pot and rockwool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Rotala Rotundifolia
  • Scientific name — Rotala rotundifolia
  • Also known as — Round-leaved Rotala, Pink Sprite, Dwarf Rotala
  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems, roughly 4-8 in
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium to high. Color tracks light closely
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient substrate or root tabs recommended
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Color is free here, not bought. Unlike the demanding red Rotala, rotundifolia pinks up on light alone — no CO₂ and no nitrate starvation required. In a low-tech tank it stays green and healthy, which is a perfectly good outcome.
  • The leaves you receive are emersed-grown and rounder. Submerged growth comes in narrower and often pinker — the plant hasn't been mislabeled, it has changed form.
  • Trim the tops and replant them. Repeated topping is what turns six stems into a dense hedge.
  • Plant stems individually an inch apart. Bunched, the lower stems shade out and drop leaves.
  • Fast growth makes it a useful nutrient sponge in a new tank, competing with algae while slower plants establish.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Rotala Care Guide.

Notes

  • Pictures are not the actual plants you will receive, but a sample representation. Unless specific, we don't guarantee aquatic plants will be free of pests, and pesticides, grow emerged or submerge.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Bacopa Salzmannii 'Purple'
products.body_html:
Want purple that doesn't wash out? Bacopa salzmannii 'Purple' — the Singapore variant — carries magenta to deep purple on the stems and on both leaf surfaces, including the undersides and shaded growth. Unlike standard salzmannii, it holds that color above water as well as below.

What You’ll Receive

Fresh, healthy Bacopa salzmannii 'Purple' cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in convenient planting formats:

Fresh Cut Plants: Approximately 6+ loose, fresh-cut stems without roots.
Fresh Cut Bunched: Approximately 6+ stems bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.
Fresh Cut Potted: About 6+ stems potted securely in a net pot with rockwool for stability and easy planting.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Purple Bacopa, Singapore Purple Bacopa
  • Scientific name — Bacopa salzmannii 'Purple'
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is South American
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Approx. 6+ fresh-cut stems, roughly 4-8 in
  • Mature height — 6–12 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Stronger light deepens the purple
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Keeps its purple grown emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • This is the variety that stays purple out of water. Standard Bacopa salzmannii reverts to green when grown emersed; the Singapore form does not, which makes it the one worth using in wabi-kusa, paludariums and dry start setups.
  • Lean nitrate deepens the color. A heavily fed tank pushes it toward green and leafy no matter how strong the light.
  • Propagate from tip and side cuttings and replant them into the stand. Waiting for bare lower stems to refill is slower and usually disappointing.
  • Some melt in transit is normal for emersed-grown stems. Judge the color after it has converted, not on arrival.
  • Also available as sterile Purple Vitro Culture.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Bacopa Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference; color varies considerably with lighting, CO₂ and nutrients.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Ludwigia Pantanal Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
One of the hardest reds worth growing. Ludwigia inclinata var. verticillata 'Pantanal' carries narrow needle-like leaves in whorls, coloring from pink through to fiery red — a texture and color combination almost nothing else in the hobby offers. It also demands high light, CO₂ and soft water to show it. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You'll Receive

  • 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag of Ludwigia Pantanal
  • Each bag contains multiple healthy plantlets, ready for immediate planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Ludwigia Pantanal
  • Scientific name — Ludwigia sp. 'Pantanal'
  • Also known as — Ludwigia inclinata var. verticillata 'Pantanal'
  • Origin — Pantanal wetlands, South America
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 6–14 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. High light is what produces the red
  • CO₂ — Recommended, in practice near-essential for color
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.0. Soft, low-carbonate water with good flow
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich substrate
  • Growth habit — Amphibious, but colors and forms best submerged
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower's Notes

  • Pantanal punishes instability. It reacts to swings in CO₂, light period or fertilization faster than almost any other stem plant — usually by dropping its lower leaves. Have the tank running steadily before you add it.
  • Soft water is not optional. Pantanal wants low carbonate hardness. In hard alkaline tap water it stunts at the tips whatever else you do — test KH rather than chasing a pH number.
  • Good flow matters as much as light. Stagnant water shows up as stunted tips.
  • Trim the tops and replant them — cuttings color faster than the stumps regrow. Tissue culture removes the pest risk but not the demands, so expect a short adaptation period and green early growth.
  • If this is a step too far, Ludwigia Super Red Mini gives deep red on a far more forgiving plant.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Ludwigia Care Guide.

Notes

  • Ludwigia Pantanal requires high light, CO₂, and a nutrient-rich environment to display its red hues. Expect a short adaptation period after planting.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Cryptocoryne Pink Flamingo Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Want genuine pink rather than red? Cryptocoryne wendtii 'Pink Flamingo' is one of the few aquarium plants that delivers it — wavy, textured leaves in light pink to rose on a compact rosette. It is also one of the most demanding Crypts in the hobby, and worth understanding before you buy.

What You’ll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing healthy Cryptocoryne 'Pink Flamingo' plantlets — ready to rinse, acclimate, and plant in your aquarium.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pink Flamingo Crypt
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne wendtii 'Pink Flamingo'
  • Also known as — Crypt Flamingo, Cryptocoryne Pink Panther
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Sri Lanka
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 3–5 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Medium to high. Strong light intensifies the pink
  • CO₂ — Recommended. It holds color and compact form far better with it
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Substrate runners, slowly

Grower’s Notes

  • The pink is why it is difficult. Pink leaves carry far less chlorophyll than green ones, so this plant photosynthesizes less efficiently than any standard wendtii and has much less margin for poor light, unstable conditions or neglect. Treat it as an advanced plant regardless of how easy ordinary Crypt Wendtii is.
  • Expect a heavy melt. All Crypts shed leaves on a change of conditions, and Pink Flamingo does it harder than most. Leave it alone for three to four weeks and let it rebuild from the roots — pulling it up is what turns a recoverable melt into a loss.
  • Feed at the roots and don't move it. Crypts melt again every time they are relocated, and this one is slow enough that a second melt costs months.
  • New growth often returns greener before the pink comes back. Judge the color once it has settled, not on the first leaves.

Three ways to buy this plant. This listing is the 4-inch Vitro Culture® bag — several sterile plantlets, the best value per plant. There is also an established bare-root or potted plant if you want size now, and a small Vitro Culture® cup with one small rooted plant — the cheapest way in, and the slowest.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Cryptocoryne Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are sample representations. Actual coloration may vary depending on lighting, CO₂, and nutrient availability. Melting may occur during the transition to submerged growth, but healthy regrowth is expected under stable care.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Ludwigia Tornado Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Ludwigia Tornado is the stem plant that looks like it is caught mid-spin. Each narrow leaf twists into a corkscrew as it grows, so a planted group reads as motion rather than a flat wall of foliage. Color runs olive-green to rust and red depending on how hard the tank is driven.

What You'll Receive

Fresh, healthy Ludwigia Tornado Vitro Culture® cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in multiple value packs:

  • 1 Bag: One 4-inch Vitro Culture® bag filled with many small plantlets
  • 5 Bags: Five 4-inch Vitro Culture® bags (excellent for larger aquascapes or propagation)
  • 10 Bags: Ten 4-inch Vitro Culture® bags (ideal for larger tank coverage)

Each 4-inch bag contains multiple young plants, which can be separated and grown into numerous individual stems—offering exceptional value and flexibility for aquascaping.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Tornado Ludwigia
  • Scientific name — Ludwigia inclinata var. verticillata 'Curly'
  • Also known as — Ludwigia Twister, Ludwigia Curly
  • Origin — Central and South America
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — 4-inch bag of small plantlets, straight-leaved on arrival
  • Mature height — 6-14 inches
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs, plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious stem, feeds from roots and water column
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • The curl is a light response, not a fixed trait. Under medium light the leaves loosen and flatten out. Strong light directly overhead is what tightens them into the spiral this variety is sold for.
  • Expect straight leaves out of the bag. Tissue culture plantlets are grown emersed and arrive without the twist. The curled form appears on the new submersed growth over the following few weeks.
  • Iron drives the red. Without a comprehensive micronutrient dose the plant grows well but stays green. Regular iron dosing under strong light is what pushes the color toward rust and wine red.
  • Separate the culture into small clusters. Rinse the gel away and plant two or three plantlets per spot, spaced about an inch apart. Planting the whole mat as one lump kills the center.
  • Trim the tops, replant them, discard the base. Like most Ludwigia, older lower stems go leggy. Cutting the top few inches and replanting them keeps the group dense and evenly colored. Also available as fresh-cut stems.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Ludwigia Care Guide.

Notes

  • Appearance may vary depending on growing conditions. Plants may arrive in emersed form and will transition to submerged growth once planted in your aquarium. Some initial leaf melt may occur during acclimation.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Aponogeton Boivinianus
products.body_html:
Heavily textured leaves with real presence. Aponogeton boivinianus is a Madagascar bulb plant producing long, deeply crinkled, dark green leaves — the most strongly textured foliage in the genus. It makes an immediate centerpiece in a larger tank.

What You'll Receive

Healthy Aponogeton Boivinianus cultivated by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in two variants:

  • Bulb Only: A firm, healthy bulb ready to sprout
  • Sprouted Bulb with Leaf: A healthy bulb with approximately 3–4 new sprouting leaves, already showing active growth

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Boivin's Aponogeton
  • Scientific name — Aponogeton boivinianus
  • Family — Aponogetonaceae
  • Origin — Madagascar
  • Plant type — Bulb / tuber
  • Foliage — Long, heavily crinkled, deep green
  • Placement — Midground to background; centerpiece in larger aquascapes
  • Growth rate — Medium to fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Not required; recommended for stronger growth
  • Water — 72–82°F; soft to moderately hard
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Propagation — Bulb division

Grower's Notes

  • The texture is the reason to buy it. Boivinianus carries the heaviest crinkling in the genus, and it holds that texture at size — where many textured plants smooth out as the leaves mature. Site it where side lighting rakes across the leaf.
  • Set the bulb on the substrate, don't bury it. Leave the top third exposed; buried bulbs rot.
  • A dormant rest is normal. The plant dies back and returns. Leave the bulb in place.
  • Minor leaf melt during acclimation is expected as it converts to your water. New growth follows.
  • Root tabs matter. A large fast-growing bulb plant runs through its reserves quickly and then stalls in inert gravel.

Notes

  • Growth rate, leaf size, and overall appearance may vary depending on aquarium conditions. Minor leaf melt can occur during acclimation.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Bucephalandra Red Catherine
products.body_html:
Red Catherine is one of the darker Bucephalandra varieties we grow — narrow, elongated leaves that hold a red-to-bronze tone rather than the blue-green of the common Buce types. It stays small, grows slowly, and needs no substrate at all.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose Bare-Root or Potted plants:

  • 1 Bare-Root: Approximately 6+ leaves
  • 5 Bare-Root: Approximately 30+ leaves total
  • 10 Bare-Root: Approximately 60+ leaves total
  • 1 Potted: Approximately 10+ leaves
  • 5 Potted: Approximately 50+ leaves total
  • 10 Potted: Approximately 100+ leaves total

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Red Catherine Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Red Catherine'
  • Also known as — Buce Red Catherine
  • Origin — Borneo (genus range)
  • Placement — Midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 3-5 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Stronger light deepens the red and bronze tones; it will still grow under low light, just greener.
  • CO₂ — Not required. Improves growth rate and color if you already run it.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed. Epiphyte; feeds from the water column.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rhizome creeper; grows submersed or emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie the horizontal rhizome to wood or rock and leave it exposed. Buried rhizomes rot.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.
  • Some leaf melt after shipping is normal. The rhizome survives it and pushes new submersed leaves within a few weeks — don't throw the plant away.
  • Red Catherine's color sits in the leaf itself rather than in a surface sheen, so it reads red across a wider range of viewing angles than the iridescent varieties.
  • Growth is slow enough that it rarely needs trimming. Plan the placement once and leave it.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Bucephalandra Care Guide.

Notes

Like most Bucephalandra, minor leaf melt may occur after introduction as the plant adjusts to new water parameters. This is normal and temporary — new submersed leaves regrow from the rhizome once the plant stabilizes.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Aponogeton Madagascariensis (Madagascar Lace)
products.body_html:
Leaves with the tissue missing. Aponogeton madagascariensis grows foliage that is pure lattice — a skeleton of veins with open holes where leaf blade would normally be. No other aquarium plant looks remotely like it. It is also genuinely demanding: cool, clean, moving water, and patience.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as Bare-root Plants, Sprouts Bulb With Leaf, or Bulb Without Leaf:
  • Bare-root Plants: A healthy loose specimen without bulb
  • Sprouted Bulb with Leaf: A healthy bulb with at least two lace leaf already growing
  • Bulb Only (No Leaf): A firm, viable bulb without current foliage (ideal for patient aquarists)

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Madagascar Lace Plant
  • Scientific name — Aponogeton madagascariensis
  • Origin — Slow rivers and lakes of Madagascar
  • Plant type — Bulb / tuber
  • Placement — Background or centerpiece
  • Mature height — 10–16 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Medium to high, but indirect. Harsh light burns the open leaf structure
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68–75°F · pH 6.0–7.0. The temperature ceiling is the strictest of any plant we sell
  • Flow — Gentle to moderate, well oxygenated. Stagnant water rots the bulb
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — True aquatic. Does not grow emersed
  • Propagation — Bulb offsets

Grower’s Notes

  • Temperature is what kills it. Above about 75°F the lace plant declines regardless of everything else. In a standard tropical community tank at 78–82°F it will not survive long — this plant needs a cool, well-oxygenated tank of its own terms.
  • Clean water matters more than fertilizer. The open leaf structure traps detritus and grows algae easily; steady flow and regular water changes keep it clear.
  • Expect a dormancy. Lace plants often drop all their leaves and rest for weeks or months. Leave the bulb in place — it usually restarts.
  • Press the bulb only partly into the substrate; fully buried bulbs rot.
  • Buy the sprouted bulb if you want certainty. A bare bulb is cheaper but asks for patience with no guarantee.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Aponogeton Care Guide.

Notes

  • This is a sensitive and specialty plant not suited for beginners. Water quality, cool temperature, and stable parameters are key to long-term success. Bulbs may take time to adjust after shipping — please plant with care and patience.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Hydrocotyle Tripartita
products.body_html:
Want a carpet with recognizable leaves? Hydrocotyle tripartita creeps across the substrate on fine stems carrying bright green clover-shaped leaves — far more distinct at a glance than the grass and moss textures most carpets offer. It also climbs, which is where it gets interesting.

What You’ll Receive

Choose the format that suits your aquascaping needs:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Loose, freshly cut portion without root, ready to be planted or attached
  • Bunched Plants: Fresh-cut stems without root bundled with foam and plant weight for easy anchoring
  • Potted Plants: Fresh-cut stems without root potted in rockwool and net pot for stable placement and easy handling

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Hydrocotyle Japan
  • Scientific name — Hydrocotyle tripartita
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 2–4 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium to high. Strong light keeps it flat; weak light makes it climb
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Creeping runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Light decides whether it carpets or climbs. Under strong light reaching the substrate it stays flat and spreads sideways. Under weaker light it grows upward, scrambling over rock and wood — which some aquascapers do on purpose for a vine effect.
  • Trim it often. It grows fast and will smother slower neighbors within weeks if left — this is a plant that needs managing, not a set-and-forget carpet.
  • Replant the trimmings. Every cut piece roots readily, so one portion covers a foreground quickly at no extra cost.
  • It attaches loosely to hardscape as it creeps, so you can wrap it around stone and let it hold on by itself.

Looking for the smaller version? Read our comparison of Hydrocotyle Tripartita vs Tripartita Mini.

Notes

  • As live plants, appearance may vary slightly. Fresh-cut and bunched plants may not have established roots but will develop quickly under stable aquarium conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Amazon Sword (Small Size)
products.body_html:
The same Amazon Sword, bought small. Echinodorus bleheri ships here at 4-6 inches — a cheaper way into a plant that will still reach a foot and a half, and a size that suits a newly planted tank where a full specimen would look out of scale from day one.

What You'll Receive

Fresh, healthy Amazon Sword (Small Size) (Echinodorus bleheri) cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®.

Available in multiple growth forms:

  • Bare-root Plant — one healthy bare-root plant approximately 4–6 inches tall
  • Rooted Bunched — one rooted bunch containing approximately 1–2 healthy plants, secured with aquarium-safe foam and a plant weight
  • Rooted Potted — one healthy rooted plant grown in a nursery pot for easy planting

Simply plant the roots into a nutrient-rich substrate while keeping the crown (where the leaves emerge) above the substrate surface.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Amazon Sword, also known as Broad Leaf Amazon Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus bleheri
  • Also known as — Echinodorus grisebachii 'Bleherae'
  • Origin — South America
  • Placement — Midground while young, background or centerpiece once grown
  • Shipped size — 4-6 inches
  • Mature height — 12-20 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner, provided you feed the roots
  • Light — Medium. It reaches full size without high-output lighting.
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required. Steady growth either way.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — root tabs are not optional in inert gravel.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette; also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on aerial floral stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Small is the shipping size, not the plant. This will not stay 4-6 inches. Under normal aquarium conditions it becomes the same 12-20 inch rosette as the full-size listing — so plant it where a large plant can live, not where a small one fits.
  • Feed it at the roots from the start. A young sword in inert gravel yellows, thins and develops holes in the older leaves. Root tabs or aquasoil under the crown are what turn a small plant into a large one.
  • Give it three inches of substrate depth. Set the crown at the surface, never below. The root mass gets substantial and a shallow bed stunts it permanently.
  • It propagates by floral stalk, not runner. Once settled it throws a tall stalk carrying plantlets. Leave each attached until it has four or five leaves and its own roots, then cut it free and plant it.
  • Expect a transition. Grown emersed, so some arriving leaves may die back as it converts to submerged growth. New leaves follow from the crown.

Other ways to buy this plant. Standard grade is the Amazon Sword; there is also a mother plant at 16-24 inches and a bulk pack.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Amazon Sword Care Guide.

Notes

Pictures are representative samples only. Live aquatic plants are natural products and may vary in size, color, and fullness depending on season and growing conditions. Plants are shipped approximately 4–6 inches tall and will continue to grow significantly larger under proper aquarium conditions. Amazon Sword is commonly grown emersed and may experience a normal transition period as it adapts to submerged aquarium conditions.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

featured_image.alt: Amazon Sword (Small Size) aquarium plant, photo 2

products.title: Bucephalandra Petite Blue Chili Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Petite Blue Chili is a nano Bucephalandra with an unusually wide color range — blue, violet, green and metallic tones that develop once the plant converts to submersed growth and shift with the tank it is in. At one to three inches it works as detail rather than mass.

What You'll Receive

  • One sealed 4-inch Vitro Culture® tissue culture bag
  • Approximately 4 small plantlets grown in sterile nutrient gel
  • 100% free from snails, algae, pesticides and pathogens
  • Rinse the gel away and separate the plantlets before planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Petite Blue Chili Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Petite Blue Chili'
  • Also known as — Buce Blue Chili
  • Origin — Borneo (genus range)
  • Placement — Foreground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 1-3 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Leaves this small have no margin for algae, so keep it down.
  • CO₂ — Not required. Deepens color and speeds growth if you already run it.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed. Epiphyte; attaches to rock or driftwood.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rhizome creeper; grows submersed or emersed. Can flower year-round.
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Gentle flow suits it, mirroring the river it comes from. Bucephalandra are rheophytes — they grow on rock in moving water. Current keeps debris off the leaves, but too much lifts a small rhizome off its mount before the roots grip.
  • Rinse the gel off completely and separate the four plantlets before attaching. Leftover nutrient agar clouds water and feeds algae.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie it to wood or rock and leave it exposed; buried rhizomes rot.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.
  • Color is a property of your tank as much as the plant. Blue and violet develop over weeks under the right spectrum; under warm white the same plant reads plain green.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Bucephalandra Care Guide.

Notes

Disclaimer: Pictures are not the actual plants you will receive, but a sample representation. Unless specific, we don't guarantee aquatic plants will be free of pests, and pesticides, grow emerged, or submerge.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Micro Sword Narrow Leaf
products.body_html:
Micro Sword Narrow Leaf is the finest-bladed of the Lilaeopsis carpets. Where the standard micro sword reads as short grass, this one reads as fine turf — thin, upright blades that spread by runner into a low meadow with a much more delicate scale.

What You'll Receive

Choose the format that best suits your planting style:

  • Bare-root Plants — Small loose clusters, ideal for direct planting and precise spacing across the foreground.
  • Rooted Bunched Plants — Healthy rooted stems tied with weight for fast anchoring and easy placement.
  • Rooted Potted Plants — Fully rooted plants grown in rockwool, the easiest to plant and fastest to establish.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Narrow Leaf Micro Sword
  • Scientific name — Lilaeopsis mauritiana
  • Also known as — Micro Sword Narrow Leaf, Mauritius Micro Sword
  • Origin — Mauritius
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Mature height — 1-3 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; this is a root feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower's Notes

  • Split it into small plugs and space them out. Separate the portion into clusters of a few blades with roots attached and plant them an inch apart. Lilaeopsis fills the gaps by runner far faster than one clump grows outward.
  • It is slow to start and then steady. Expect very little visible progress for the first three or four weeks while the roots establish, then runners in every direction. Do not disturb it during the quiet phase.
  • Feed the roots. This carpet takes almost everything from the substrate. On inert sand without root tabs it survives but barely spreads; over aquasoil it closes properly.
  • Light reaches the base or the base dies. Once the carpet thickens, trim it back. Shaded lower blades brown off, lose grip and the mat lifts in patches.
  • Finer than standard micro sword. If you have used Lilaeopsis brasiliensis and found it coarse for a nano tank, this is the version to use — same habit, noticeably thinner blades.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference only. Actual plant size and density may vary. Some initial transition melting may occur as the plant adapts to submerged growth.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Fissidens Nobilis
products.body_html:
Feathers, not fuzz. Fissidens nobilis grows flat, distinctly feather-shaped fronds in a single plane — and at a noticeably larger scale than Phoenix Moss, so the individual fronds are visible rather than merging into a mass. The most structured-looking moss we carry.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a small loose portion
  • Approx. 2" x 2" in size
  • Perfect to attached to driftwood, rock, or stone

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Noble Fissidens
  • Scientific name — Fissidens nobilis
  • Placement — Foreground, attached to driftwood, stone or décor
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required, though it thickens growth
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Fragmentation — divide and re-attach

Grower’s Notes

  • Frond size is what you're paying for. Most mosses read as texture from a distance. Nobilis is large enough that the feather shape stays legible — use it where it will be seen up close, not as background filler.
  • Tie it thinly and flat. The fronds grow in one plane, so pressing it flat against wood or stone gives the best result; a thick pad hides the structure and rots underneath.
  • Slow growth means it holds its shape for months without trimming — but also that algae, once in it, is very hard to clear.
  • Keep light moderate and flow steady; stagnant corners let detritus settle between the fronds.
  • Divide with scissors and re-attach the pieces — each fragment establishes independently.

Want to go deeper? Read our guide to aquarium moss varieties and how to attach them.

Notes

  • Pictures are not the actual plants you will receive, but a sample representation. Unless specific, we don't guarantee aquatic plants will be free of pests, pesticides, grow emerged, or submerge.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.
